title: Google AI Research Releases Agile Deliberation Framework for Gray-Area Image Classifiers
abstract: Google Research has released Agile Deliberation , a human-in-the-loop framework for building image classifiers around subjective concepts. Think ‘healthy food’, ‘inspiring artwork’ or clickbait in content moderation. Most tooling assumes users already know the concept boundary. Agile Deliberation assumes they do not, and helps them find it. Agile Deliberation is a Google Research’s framework that turns a vague concept into a structured written definition. That definition does two jobs. It is a human-readable policy, and it is the text prompt for a VLM classifier. Each round keeps the candidate definition with the best F1 on the user’s labels. The design came from interviews with a group of content moderation experts . Experts scoped a concept first, then refined it on borderline images. Finding those images was the slow part. Stage 1 breaks the concept into at most 3 unit concepts, using prompt chaining with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Each unit gets candidate positive and negative subconcepts, shown with retrieved images. For healthy food, positives might be salads or grain bowls. Negatives might be processed food or raw, unprepared ingredients. The user keeps, flips or drops each one. Stage 2 skips classic uncertainty sampling. The classifier is a prompted generative VLM, so its confidence scores are often uncalibrated. Instead, the system hunts for images that are borderline in meaning. Users label each image and add short notes on disagreements. An LLM turns those notes into candidate definitions. A greedy update keeps the best-scoring one. Subjective concepts have no fixed ground truth, so Google team skipped static benchmarks. It ran 18 live sessions of about 90 minutes each. 9 participants without professional moderation experience did 2 sessions each. One session used Agile Deliberation, the other used manual deliberation. Each participant spent about 45 minutes defining a concept, then labeled 200 held-out test images. The two concepts were ‘paid to play’ clickbait and ‘healthy food’. Retrieval ran over a proprietary 100M-image dataset and WebLI, respectively. Source: Table 1 of the CVPR 2026 paper . F1 averaged over participants. The repo ships a Demo.ipynb that walks through the healthy food example. It needs a Gemini API key and defaults to gemini-2.5-pro and gemini-2.5-flash. A setup script builds a FAISS index over LAION-400M CLIP embeddings. The default 2 shards take about 260 MB. All 100 shards take about 13 GB. title: webAI Releases TwIL-8B, an 8.8B Reasoning Model Scoring 98.2 on MATH-500
abstract: webAI has released TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s launch post frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference. TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has 40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a <think> block before each answer. It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer. Balanced is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces. Verbose reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems. TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were 1.7B and 3B formal-logic models released in August 2026. webAI used 3 post-training stages : Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals. All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only. Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11. Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer. Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional. TwIL-8B figures from the model card . † = verbose variant. All scores self-reported by each vendor unless marked. from_pretrained("webAI-Official/TwIL-8B") loads the balanced variant. Pass subfolder="verbose" for the verbose one. The model card lists GGUF builds for llama.cpp: Give it a large generation budget. The card’s example sets max_new_tokens=32768 . A short budget truncates reasoning and scores far worse. All reported scores used bf16 weights, so expect small drops at Q4_K_M. No hosted inference provider serves the model on Hugging Face yet. title: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
abstract: Ricursive Intelligence just released Ripple-65B Preview . Ripple-65B Preview is a 65B dense open-weight model from Ricursive, pretrained from scratch for agentic coding. It is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive’s AI chip design platform. The main claim: 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 , the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. Every MoE rival it beats on that test carries 501B to 975B total parameters. The release includes 3 checkpoints : an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version , and a BF16 base model . All ship under Apache 2.0. Pretraining used a text-only corpus, mostly English and code, at 8K sequence length. Ricursive team states that the full R&D cost was $32M . That figure covers ladder experiments, data mixing, evals, synthetic data and the final runs. Ricursive team estimates that it is one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity. Training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization. The model is thin and deep: a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. It moves from Olmo 3’s Llama-like layout to a Gemma 3N-like design for stability. Key choices: Ricursive team built the recipe through laddering experiments starting from Olmo 3’s ladder . It rejected changes that failed to hold at 4B scale, such as 2-stream mHC. The technical post reports a 16x code compute-efficiency gain at 4B scale. Post-training ran midtraining, long context, SFT, long-context SFT and mixed RL. Long-context stages trained at 2M sequence length. Ricursive bought no post-training data and built its own synthetic pipelines. The RL recipe combines truncated importance sampling , score centering and a linear length penalty . Ripple hit 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts. Ricursive puts that at roughly 70x fewer than Beam, which reported over 100M rollouts . Ricursive team ran missing evals in-house using OpenCode, and Terminus 2 for SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard and DeepSWE 1.1. Scores below are Ricursive’s presented data. Ricursive team also reran Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K. Most rivals dropped there; Beam fell to 70.8. Muse Spark Open rose to 78.7, still below Ripple’s 80.5. Ripple scores from the Ricursive model card . Competitor scores from each vendor’s own source. All self-reported. Weights are on Hugging Face . Ricursive lists Together AI , GMI Cloud and OpenRouter at launch, with Fireworks later. Together AI’s page currently marks the model as coming soon. On datacenter GPUs, the model reaches 250 tok/s on 2x B200 at batch 8, before quantization. The experimental NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes MLP layers and keeps attention in BF16. Ricursive team positions it for local devices like NVIDIA DGX Spark. A DFlash2 variant is also listed. Check out the the launch blog , the model card and the NVFP4 checkpoint . title: Web Scraping 7,000 Pages in 3 Minutes with Python and Olostep
abstract: Web Scraping 7,000 Pages in 3 Minutes with Python and Olostep Scrape thousands of pages in a few minutes with the Olostep Batch API, download Markdown, and measure what actually finished. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 5, 2026 in Python Scraping thousands of web pages can take hours, especially when you are collecting data for enterprise applications, market research, price monitoring, or large-scale AI systems. The challenge is not just scraping pages quickly, but making sure the process is reliable, scalable, and easy to manage. I wanted to see how fast I could scrape 10,000 web pages using Python and the Olostep Batch API . In my test, 7,225 pages were processed in under 3 minutes , which was impressive. However, completing the entire job, including scraping, downloading, and verifying the results, took 22 minutes and 26 seconds. Out of 10,000 URLs, 9,938 were successfully saved as Markdown files. In this tutorial, I will show you how to use Python and Olostep to scrape thousands of pages in a single batch, track progress, download the content, and verify the results. I will also share the actual performance numbers, including what worked well and where the process slowed down. Understanding How the Olostep Batch API Works The Olostep Batch API lets you scrape up to 10,000 URLs in a single batch instead of sending thousands of individual requests. It handles the processing while you track progress, retrieve completed results, and download the extracted content. Olostep is also expanding beyond developer-focused scraping tools to provide web data infrastructure for enterprises . According to its co-founder, the platform can process 100,000 pages in under 25 minutes for enterprise workloads. This kind of scale is useful for companies that regularly collect large amounts of web data for market research, competitor monitoring, product intelligence, and AI applications. For this tutorial, I used the Olostep Python SDK to scrape 10,000 MDN documentation pages and save their content as Markdown files. The workflow involves five steps: Prepare the URLs: Download the MDN sitemap and select 10,000 unique pages. Submit the batch: Send all URLs to Olostep in a single job. Track progress: Monitor completed pages until scraping finishes. Download the results: Retrieve the processed content and save it as Markdown. Verify the files: Check the saved files, identify missing results, and measure the total execution time. The workflow diagram below shows the complete process, from collecting URLs to verifying the final output. One important thing to understand is that a completed batch does not necessarily mean every page was successfully saved . In my test, 9,938 out of 10,000 pages were saved, with 62 missing. This is why verifying the results matters just as much as scraping speed, especially when building reliable data pipelines. Scraping 10,000 Pages with the Olostep Batch API We will use the Olostep Batch API to scrape 10,000 MDN documentation pages, download their content as Markdown files, and verify how many pages were successfully collected. For this experiment, I used Python 3.13.15 and Olostep SDK 1.2.2 . The process is divided into six steps, from setting up the environment to checking the final results. You will need an Olostep API key to follow along. You can either set it as an environment variable ( OLOSTEP_API_KEY ) or enter it securely when prompted. Note: Submitting a new batch consumes API credits, so make sure your account has sufficient credits before running the code. 1. Install the SDK Start by opening a new Jupyter Notebook or launching the notebook provided with this tutorial. In the first cell, install the Olostep Python SDK, along with requests for fetching the MDN sitemap and tqdm for tracking scraping progress. %pip -q install olostep==1.2.2 requests tqdm 2. Configure the Client Next, we will set up the Olostep client using our API key, create a folder to store the scraped data, and define a few helper functions to save and validate the results. We will also add a small workaround for a response-handling issue in SDK version 1.2.2 to make sure we can check the batch status without errors. import asyncio, csv, gzip, hashlib, json, os, random, time from datetime import datetime, timezone from getpass import getpass from pathlib import Path from xml.etree import ElementTree as ET import requests from olostep import AsyncOlostep from olostep.errors import OlostepClientError_ResponseValidationFailed from olostep.models.response import BatchInfoResponse from tqdm import tqdm N = 10000 MAX_WAIT_SECONDS = 2400 DATA = Path("data"); DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True) client = AsyncOlostep(api_key=os.getenv("OLOSTEP_API_KEY") or getpass("Olostep API key: ")) def write_json(path, value): path.write_text(json.dumps(value, indent=2), encoding="utf-8") def valid_file(path): try: return path.is_file() and bool(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()) except (OSError, UnicodeError): return False async def batch_info(batch_id): try: return await client.batches.info(batch_id) except OlostepClientError_ResponseValidationFailed as error: return BatchInfoResponse.model_validate({"parser": "none", **json.loads(error.response.body)}) 3. Build the URL Dataset Now, we will download the MDN sitemap and randomly select 10,000 unique documentation pages for our experiment. The code saves these URLs in a CSV file so we can reuse the same list without downloading it again. It also checks for duplicates and makes sure we are working with the correct dataset. source = "https://developer.mozilla.org/sitemaps/en-us/sitemap.xml.gz" if not (DATA / "urls.csv").exists(): response = requests.get(source, timeout=60); response.raise_for_status() payload = response.content xml = gzip.decompress(payload) if payload.startswith(b"\x1f\x8b") else payload (DATA / "mdn_sitemap.xml").write_bytes(xml) ns = {"s": "http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"} nodes = ET.fromstring(xml).findall("s:url", ns) urls = sorted({node.findtext("s:loc", namespaces=ns) for node in nodes}) urls = [url for url in urls if url and url.startswith("https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/")] random.Random(42).shuffle(urls) assert len(urls) >= N, f"Only {len(urls)} unique documentation URLs available." with (DATA / "urls.csv").open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: writer = csv.writer(f); writer.writerow(["url"]); writer.writerows([url] for url in urls[:N]) write_json(DATA / "dataset.json", {"source": source, "downloaded_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), "available_urls": len(urls), "selected_urls": N, "random_seed": 42}) with (DATA / "urls.csv").open(encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f: urls = [row["url"] for row in csv.DictReader(f)] assert len(urls) == len(set(urls)) == N fingerprint = hashlib.sha256("\n".join(urls).encode()).hexdigest() expected = {f"{i:05d}": url for i, url in enumerate(urls)} print(f"Ready: {len(urls):,} unique URLs; source: {source}") Output: Ready: 10,000 unique URLs; source: https://developer.mozilla.org/sitemaps/en-us/sitemap.xml.gz The output confirms that our dataset contains 10,000 unique URLs, ready for batch scraping. 4. Submit and Monitor the Batch Next, we will submit all 10,000 URLs to Olostep in a single batch and monitor the scraping progress using a progress bar. The code also saves the batch ID, allowing us to resume the same job instead of starting over if the process gets interrupted. checkpoint = Path("batch.json") resumed = checkpoint.exists() if resumed: run = json.loads(checkpoint.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) assert run["urls_sha256"] == fingerprint, "URL list changed; preserve the checkpoint before starting another batch." else: started = time.time() batch = await client.batches.create(urls=[{"url": url, "custom_id": key} for key, url in expected.items()]) run = {"batch_id": batch.

title: What I Did with Hermes Agent, Ollama & Local Models
abstract: What I Did with Hermes Agent, Ollama & Local Models Build a local multi-agent travel planner with Hermes Agent and Ollama: a coordinator and three specialist agents that research destinations, suggest stays, and generate real Google Flights search links. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 5, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence I wanted an AI agent that could actually help me plan a trip, research a destination, suggest where to stay, and find a real flight — without a subscription, without sending every question to a cloud provider, and without a monthly bill creeping up the more I used it. That search led me to two tools worth knowing: Hermes Agent and Ollama . This article is the real project that came out of pairing them: a working, tested, multi-agent travel research team running entirely on my own hardware. Before the build, though, it's worth actually understanding the two tools doing the work, since most of what makes this project possible traces back to what each one is specifically good at. Introducing Hermes Agent Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent built by Nous Research , released under the permissive MIT license and currently at version 0.21.1 as of this writing. It ships in two ways: a native desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux, and a terminal-first CLI. Both give you the same underlying agent, not a stripped-down version. What separates Hermes from an ordinary chatbot is genuine agentic capability. It can read and edit real files on your machine, run terminal commands, and browse the live web, which is the exact combination this travel project depends on: an agent that can search for current destination information and act on what it finds, not just describe what it would do. A few features matter specifically for a project like this one. Multi-agent orchestration lets a coordinator agent delegate specific tasks to specialist sub-agents and combine their results, which is the entire architecture behind the travel team built later in this article. Persistent memory means Hermes can remember details across sessions — a stated budget, a past trip, a travel style — rather than starting from zero every time you open it. Its Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool support connects it to any MCP server, including a sandboxed web search tool run in its own isolated container, and its custom tool support means you're not limited to what ships built in, which is how the real flight search tool later in this article gets wired in at all. Understanding Ollama and Local Models Hermes needs a language model to actually think with, and that's Ollama's job. Ollama is an open-source tool that downloads, manages, and serves large language models directly on your own computer, exposing them through a local API that behaves exactly like a cloud provider's, just pointed at localhost instead of the internet. That detail is what makes the whole pairing work: because Ollama's API is OpenAI-compatible , Hermes can talk to a model running entirely on your machine using the same integration path it would use for any cloud model. " Local models " is the other half of this worth understanding plainly. Rather than sending your questions and files to a company's servers and getting billed per token, you run an open-weight model — one whose underlying parameters are published and downloadable — entirely on your own CPU or GPU. Nothing leaves your machine except the specific web searches your agent decides to run, and there's no usage bill, since the only cost is the electricity your computer uses while it's thinking. The trade-off is honest and worth stating plainly too: a local model on consumer hardware won't match a frontier cloud model's raw capability, and it'll typically run slower, especially without a GPU. For a project like the one in this article — research, planning, tool use — that trade-off is a genuinely good deal. With both tools explained, here's the real project they're being used to build. Sketching the Idea The project — call it Wanderlist — works like this: tell it where you want to go, and a coordinated team of local AI agents researches the destination, suggests notable places, points you toward well-regarded places to stay, and hands you a real, ready-to-use flight search link. No request leaves your machine except the actual web searches involved, and there's no subscription or API key beyond what's genuinely free. Four real jobs, one for each team member: research the destination and its current entry requirements, suggest what's actually worth seeing, point toward reputable accommodation guidance, and generate a real flight search a person can click and use immediately. Checking Prerequisites and Installing Ollama The hardware requirement that actually matters here is being able to run a model with real tool-calling support, since a travel research team that can search the web and call custom tools needs a model genuinely capable of both. Component Minimum Recommended RAM 8 GB 24+ GB (for a 31B-class model) Storage 5 GB free 25+ GB CPU 4 cores 8+ cores GPU Not required NVIDIA GPU with 8+ GB VRAM Install Ollama: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh Pull a model with real tool-calling support. The same reasoning from earlier applies here: a model without it can chat, but it can't actually delegate tasks or call a custom tool, which is the entire point of a multi-agent team. ollama pull gemma4:31b Code explanation: gemma4:31b is worth the extra RAM specifically because this project delegates work between four separate agents and calls a custom Python tool, both of which require a model that reliably understands when and how to invoke a tool, not just produce fluent text. Configuring Hermes to Use Your Local Model Point Hermes at Ollama's local endpoint in ~/.hermes/config.yaml : model: default: "gemma4:31b" provider: "custom" base_url: "http://localhost:11434/v1" Code explanation: provider: "custom" tells Hermes to treat this as a generic OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and base_url points it at Ollama running locally on port 11434. No API key is needed, since Ollama doesn't check for one. Designing the Travel Team: A Coordinator and Three Specialists This is the real architecture. A root coordinator receives the trip request and delegates to three specialists, each with a narrow, well-defined job. agents: root: description: "Travel planning coordinator" instruction: | You are a travel planning coordinator. When given a trip request, delegate destination research to destination-scout, accommodation guidance to stay-finder, and flight options to flight-finder. Combine their findings into one clear trip briefing. sub_agents: [destination-scout, stay-finder, flight-finder] toolsets: - type: think - type: memory path: ./trip_preferences.db destination-scout: description: "Researches destinations, attractions, and entry requirements" instruction: | Search the web for current information on the requested destination: notable places to visit, best time of year, and any visa or entry requirements. Always search fresh for entry requirements, never answer from memory, since these change and being wrong has real consequences for travelers. Cite where each fact came from. toolsets: - type: mcp ref: docker:duckduckgo stay-finder: description: "Finds well-regarded neighborhoods and accommodation types" instruction: | Search the web for current, well-regarded recommendations on where to stay in the destination, neighborhoods, accommodation styles, and typical price ranges from recent travel sources. Never invent specific listings or prices, only report what current sources actually say. toolsets: - type: mcp ref: docker:duckduckgo flight-finder: description: "Builds real flight search links and current price context" instruction: | Given an origin, destination, and travel dates, use the build_flight_search_url tool to generate a real search link.

title: AI for scientific discovery: How researchers use Claude
abstract: Chapter 01 : Summary Johannes Hermle*, Ben Jones*, Lukas Althoff*, Ryan Heller, Thomas Lyttelton, Carolyn Stein, Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory *Lead authors of the report Summary What we measure. AI could speed up scientific discovery, but by how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future. Where scientists use Claude. Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude. How Claude use tracks AI capability. We create a measure of how well AI can, in theory, perform each research task. The tasks AI is best suited to (the top 20% on this measure) get two to four times as much Claude use as the time researchers spend on them would predict. The tasks AI is least suited to (the bottom 20%), which include most physical work, get very little. We observe the same pattern across fields: fields where AI can perform many tasks well, such as computer science and statistics, use Claude more. What this could mean for the speed of scientific discovery. Using a simple model, we explore scenarios for how much AI could speed up research. If existing AI capabilities are widely adopted, they could double research output in some fields. If AI could carry out all non-physical research work, output in fields such as computer science and statistics could rise as much as 15-fold, while output in bench sciences such as chemistry and biology, which are held back by physical bottlenecks, would rise three- or fourfold. In our survey of researchers who actively use AI, about 40% expect AI models to carry out full research projects on their own by 2030. Introduction Science has been described as an “endless frontier” (Bush 1945). But how fast we explore that frontier has historically been limited by a scarce resource: the time and talent of human researchers. Artificial intelligence could ease that limit by amplifying what researchers can do, transforming both the process of discovery and the pace of exploration (Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024). Few applications of AI could matter more for human welfare. Given the highly cognitive nature of research compared with most sectors of the economy, AI’s effects may be particularly large and early in this domain. Recent examples show AI playing a growing role in scientific discovery. In structural biology, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional shapes of over 200 million proteins (Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024), and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In materials science, GNoME predicted 380,000 stable new crystals (Merchant et al. 2023). In mathematics, researchers have used AI systems to help resolve decades-old Erdős problems, produce a potential proof for a Millennium Prize problem, and make progress on other major problems, from open conjectures to verifying landmark proofs (Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026). Beyond these developments, most scientific progress involves many specialized, interlinked research tasks, which can vary substantially across fields. How much AI accelerates scientific discovery depends not only on AI’s capabilities, but also on how it is adopted across these tasks. In this report, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to study the scientific use of Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science. We document how usage varies across fields and tasks, identify what explains these usage patterns, and outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate research. Claude use in science varies by field. Relative to their number of researchers, formal sciences such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics use Claude more heavily, while health and lab-based physical sciences use it less. Across research tasks, scientists use Claude more for analyzing data and writing, and less for gathering data or generating ideas and hypotheses. This is consistent with self-reported AI use from an accompanying survey of scientists. To understand these differences, we develop a measure of theoretical AI capability. Claude use is higher in tasks and fields that score higher on this measure. These also tend to be more cognitive in nature and better suited to reinforcement learning, in which AI learns from feedback on repeated attempts. In short, scientists appear to use AI where it works best. Based on these findings, we outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate scientific progress. With current capabilities, research output in some fields could as much as double, primarily from task-level augmentation. Researchers in our survey expect much greater capabilities to come. In a hypothetical scenario where AI fully automates all non-physical work, highly cognitive fields such as computer science or statistics could see up to a 15-fold increase in output. Because the fields with the largest potential for acceleration include those that produce AI itself, these gains could create an additional feedback loop, in which faster AI research produces more capable AI, which in turn could further accelerate research. While faster scientific discovery could bring substantial benefits to humanity, AI-driven research also carries risks and uncertainties. Less human oversight could lead to the pursuit of dangerous or unethical research. AI could also reshape researchers’ careers, making research work more or less rewarding, and alter the sense of purpose associated with the human pursuit of knowledge. How we conducted this research Our goal with this research is to measure the different ways scientists use Claude while protecting the details of their work. To do this, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to analyze the scientific use of Claude on consumer plans. A language model, used here as a “classifier,” reads each session transcript and labels it with a fixed set of categories, such as the field and the research task it involves, according to a predefined taxonomy (SciNet taxonomy by Alamos and Althoff 2026). The resulting labels, such as “chemistry” or “data cleaning,” are the only information from these conversations retained and analyzed by the research team for this report. No classifier employed in this study extracts and stores open-ended information or details on research content, such as research datasets, hypotheses, experimental methods, early findings, or unpublished papers. Results are reported only in aggregate and only for cells that meet a minimum number of distinct accounts. All classifiers introduced in this study are listed in the Appendix . Our measurement involves two steps. A first classifier identifies whether a session transcript involves scientific work. A second classifier then assigns each of these transcripts to a field, subfield, and task in the SciNet taxonomy. SciNet contains 7,262 tasks, spanning 34 fields and 318 subfields.

title: Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
abstract: Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself. With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money. Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that's new to you. Like the rest of Claude , Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer. Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week, on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the US. What it looks like Say it's late in the month and payday is still 10 days away. When you ask Claude, "Where did my money go this month?" it adds up your spending across the accounts you connected and sorts it by category. In this example, that comes to $4,309.37, with more than half going to rent and utilities and $1,024.51 to food and drink. From there, you can dig deeper: "Is that more than usual?" "Anything else I'm missing?" "So what's left before payday?" Claude checks the previous months and points to a membership renewal. Then Claude tells you about four payments that will come out of your checking account before payday, and what you’ll have left: $1,393.22. If you ask whether anything looks off, Claude reads across every account you've connected and can point to what's easy to miss, like charges that hit twice, unexpected fees, or a bill that’s crept up all year. You can also ask bigger questions, like "Am I spending more than I make?" or "What's an APR, and what has mine cost me this year?" Claude explains the term, then adds up the interest you've been charged. Ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what's due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds one you can keep adjusting. Security and privacy Claude's access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn't designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank. Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid , a service that connects apps to banks. That's where you agree to its terms and approve Claude's read-only access, so Claude doesn't ask for or see your bank password. For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank's name, each account's name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren't used to train our models. For anything you share with Claude outside the hub, your privacy settings apply. You can unlink an account anytime, and then Claude can no longer see its data. More details can be found in our Privacy Center. Getting started When you see Personal Finance in Claude's sidebar, open it, connect one account, and ask a single question, like "Can I afford a trip this spring?" or "How much could I save each month?" You'll find the setup steps, and how your data is used and kept, in the Help Center. (opens in new tab) What’s next Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.

title: More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
abstract: Claude Enterprise has new security and admin features, including a security center, generally available inference hooks, centralized management, and additional access controls. To see how Claude is set up, the security center shows how your organization’s Claude settings compare with Anthropic’s recommended configuration. To apply your policies, inference hooks send prompts and tool calls to your data security tools for a check. To manage access, centralized management gives your company one admin console for company-wide settings, and new access controls let you sign members out through the Admin API, manage your IP allowlist yourself, and help prevent shadow IT by blocking personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers. We also recently announced an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) integration, which runs your organization's sensor inside the unified Claude and Cowork virtual machine on the user's computer. Security teams need to see how Claude is configured, what it does on company devices, and how data is handled as people work. These features give them that visibility and control. Security center: review your Claude security settings in one place Security teams can review Claude's security settings for chat, Cowork, and Claude Code on one page, instead of setting by setting. The security center is a new page in Organization settings that compares settings with Anthropic's recommended configuration, so your team can see what to change and where to change it. For each control, the security center shows the current value, the recommended value where there is one, and a link to the setting where you can change it. It also shows which settings are new or recently changed. The security center checks your configuration each time the page loads, so automatically checked controls reflect your current settings. Organizations with the Compliance API can read the same results through it. Attestations give your admins a shared workspace for security reviews. They can work through the process together once, recording the current state of each control, accepting risks, and flagging issues in one place. You can download the security center page as a report to share with auditors and relevant stakeholders. The report marks which controls the page checked automatically and which an Owner confirmed. The security center is guidance based on Anthropic's recommendations, not a certification or a guarantee of compliance with any law or standard. Inference hooks Inference hooks connect Claude to the data security tools your organization already uses, so your data loss prevention (DLP) and security policies can apply to prompts and tool calls as people work. There are two kinds of hooks, both now generally available: Prompt hooks send prompts from supported Claude products to your security tool for a check. Pre-tool-call hooks check tool calls in supported Claude products before they run. Hooks work with security vendors. Your team keeps the policies it has already written and applies them to Claude. Centralized management: one console for identity and access across your organization Centralized management gives your parent organization, which represents your company across its Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform organizations, its own admin console at admin.claude.com. Admins manage company-wide settings there once for the organizations under your parent, instead of from individual organization settings. These settings include single sign-on, directory sync (SCIM), domain verification, groups, and Compliance API keys. The console shows every organization under the parent in one place and adds two roles. Parent organization owners can manage everything at the parent level, including who holds the owner and admin roles. Parent organization admins can manage everything except those role assignments. Companies can also connect more than one identity provider, each with its own single sign-on and SCIM configuration. An acquired company can keep its existing provider, or your team can move to a new provider one domain at a time. Each organization keeps its own members, roles, settings, and organization-level security controls, such as IP allowlisting, tenant restrictions, and session duration. A parent role doesn't grant access inside an organization by default, but Compliance API keys created at the parent can read data across organizations. Access controls: member sign-out and shadow IT prevention Security teams can now sign a member out of Claude with a single Admin API call, without removing them from the organization. The call ends that member's sign-in sessions on every browser and device, and apps like Claude Code have to sign in again. It doesn't end API keys, cloud sessions already running, or scheduled routines, and the member can sign in again afterwards. Enterprise admins can now set up and manage their IP allowlist themselves, without going through Anthropic. An IP allowlist limits access to most Claude products to the IP addresses your organization approves. Admins can now set the most-used Claude Desktop settings, with no device management push. To help prevent shadow IT, admins can also block personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers. Owners can also limit which workspace folders people can use with Claude. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in Cowork and unified Claude When Cowork and unified Claude work locally, they run shell commands and code in an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer for additional protection. That isolation helps protect the device, and security teams have asked for the same visibility into the virtual machine that they have everywhere else on the endpoint. Admins can now run their organization's EDR sensor inside the Cowork virtual machine. The sensor reports activity there to the same console your security team already monitors. This covers the virtual machine on the user's computer, not Cowork sessions in the cloud. Admins set up the integration through device management on macOS and Windows. Each time the virtual machine starts, Claude verifies the sensor package's signature from your EDR vendor before installing it. Sensors run in detection mode: they report activity to your security team and don't block it. The integration works with supported EDR vendors, which are listed in the Help Center . Getting started These features are available for Claude Enterprise, with some exceptions during beta listed in the Help Center . The security center is in beta. Inference hooks , including prompt hooks and pre-tool-call hooks, are generally available. Admins can manage both inference hooks and the security center in Organization settings. Centralized management is also in beta. To start setup, an admin of any organization under your parent goes to admin.claude.com and proposes the parent organization admins. Admins of the other organizations review and approve, and the last approval completes setup. Setup can't be undone, so identify your parent organization admins before you start. Signing members out through the Admin API and the self-serve IP allowlist are in beta. Owners can manage Claude Desktop settings in Organization settings, also in beta. Endpoint detection and response in Cowork is in beta on macOS and Windows for Claude Team and Enterprise, and for the Claude desktop app on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, deployed through MDM for supported vendors.

title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
abstract: content type highlight published November 5, 2026 Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently. In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions , a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) — once, offline, for a fixed database of keys — that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs. The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters — k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n — keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n / k — a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below. Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid. MIPS as a Support Function What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs) . Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself. The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input. Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best: The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality. KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced. Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter. Learned Routing with SupportNet As shown in Figure 1 , the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each cluster’s centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match. If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2 , in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings. Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each cluster’s support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster. Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: “How good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?

title: Configure, Certify, and Operate Kubernetes GPU Clusters with NVIDIA DSX OS
abstract:
One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job. The node may pass basic health checks and show normal utilization, leaving operators to discover the problem only after the workload is running. These issues can appear at any point in a cluster’s lifecycle. A GPU cluster that passes readiness checks at handover changes as nodes are replaced, drivers are patched, and capacity is added. Without repeated validation, the original certification no longer reflects the cluster’s condition. This visibility gap wastes compute on failing nodes and leaves healthy nodes idle out of caution. Utilization metrics can mask these losses. Goodput, which is the volume of work successfully completed, provides a more useful measure of cluster efficiency. Maintaining cluster readiness requires validation throughout the cluster’s operational lifecycle—after configuration changes, as capacity grows, and before repaired nodes return to service. The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies for designing, building, and operating efficient, resilient AI factories. Its open source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, includes tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure. Configure : NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) establishes a reproducible baseline for GPU-optimized Kubernetes infrastructure. Defines version-locked configuration recipes for components such as networking, storage, and drivers. Renders recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools. Certify : NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) validates whether the cluster is ready to run production workloads. Tests GPUs, networking, and storage using AI workloads and diagnostics. Records certification results and helps identify faulty nodes. Operate : NVSentinel monitors cluster health and supports fault remediation and revalidation. Publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health. When configured, cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, and remediates faults. Can trigger revalidation with NVCRE before nodes return to service. All three are open source projects licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions. Before you begin, install and configure AICR , NVCRE , and NVSentinel using their installation guides. The examples assume access to a Kubernetes GPU cluster with the required CLIs, controllers, dependencies, and NVCRE test provider configured. This walkthrough follows one cluster through its lifecycle: configuration from a recipe, certification before production use, monitoring during operation, and recertification after repair. Each command is a step in that sequence. Configure: A baseline you can reproduce AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version-controlled files and renders them into artifacts your existing deployment tooling applies. It generates and validates; your deployer applies and reconciles them. Declarative templates help detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs. You describe the target environment. AICR resolves it against a library of validated overlays and emits a recipe: aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h100 --os ubuntu \ --intent inference --platform dynamo -o recipe.yaml Each component entry in the resulting recipe pins a version and declares which dependencies must be healthy before the component is installed: apiVersion: aicr.run/v1alpha2
componentRefs: - name: dynamo-platform chart: dynamo-platform namespace: dynamo-system source: https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia/ai-dynamo type: Helm version: 1.4.2 valuesFile: components/dynamo-platform/values.yaml dependencyRefs: - grove - cert-manager - kube-prometheus-stack - gpu-operator - kai-scheduler The recipe includes three key properties: Pinned versions: The version is fixed, helping you reproduce the software configuration and investigate failures. In contrast, a floating tag can point to a different software version over time, making failures harder to reproduce. A dependency graph: dependencyRefs declares what must be installed and healthy first. AICR resolves the graph when it renders the bundle, so the ordering is already encoded in the artifacts your deployer applies. You don’t need to specify that cert-manager comes before NVSentinel, and adding a component later doesn’t require renumbering. Health assertions per component: Each entry carries a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation and checks whether the component meets its configured health criteria. Kubernetes can report a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff as Running , so a check based only on the pod phase can miss a broken component. The shipped assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone. Rendering the recipe is a separate step that connects AICR to your existing pipeline: aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles --deployer accepts helm , argocd , argocd-helm , flux , or helmfile , so the same validated recipe becomes Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands. You can keep your existing deployment tooling and use AICR to generate its configuration artifacts. Because the recipe is a file, you can use version history, code review, and drift detection to manage the baseline. # Check a live cluster against the recipe's constraints
aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml # Compare a golden baseline against the live cluster, non-zero exit on drift
aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift --fail-on-drift turns the drift check into a continuous integration (CI) gate rather than a report. Certify: Prove the cluster will run the job The cluster is now built to a known baseline. It still needs workload validation. Standard health checks confirm that basic services are running. They don’t confirm that the cluster can run a demanding multinode job across its interconnect without stalling. NVCRE validates workload readiness by running training jobs and NVIDIA Collective Communication Library (NCCL) tests. NVSentinel manages validation requests, scheduling gates, quarantine, and repair, while NVCRE runs tests and records results. Table 1 shows how these responsibilities fit into the node validation lifecycle. Step Responsible component Action Outcome 1. Request and gate NVSentinel lifecycle manager; operators for upgrades or fabric changes Create a ValidationRequest for new or repaired nodes. After upgrades or fabric changes, operators cordon the nodes and create the request. A cordon or taint blocks scheduling on the nodes during validation. 2. Test and attribute NVCRE through nvcre-provider Run workloads and diagnostic tests. Bisect failing groups to identify suspect nodes. Test results identify suspect nodes. NVCRE doesn’t change the node state. 3. Record and evaluate NVCRE and NVSentinel lifecycle manager NVCRE records pass/fail results, failing node IDs, and failure reasons in the Certification resource. The lifecycle manager evaluates the results. The validation outcome determines whether the scheduling gate can be removed. 4. Resolve the gate NVSentinel lifecycle manager Remove or retain the scheduling gate based on validation results and any remaining tests. Pass: remove the configured gate once no other tests hold the node. Failure after retries: keep the node cordoned. Table 1. Node validation duties, actions, and outcomes A certification identifies the nodes to test, the categories to run, and the thresholds that determine whether the tests pass or fail: apiVersion: nvcre.nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: Certification
metadata: name: gpu-cluster-cert
spec: target: nodeSelector: nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true" categories: - domain: communication variant: nccl-all-reduce - domain: training variant: nemotron5-8b options: thresholds: busBandwidthGBps: "value >= 300" nvcrectl certification run --cert-file certification.

title: Five Ways NVIDIA Co-Design Maximizes the Value of Every Byte in the AI Factory
abstract: In an AI factory, high bandwidth memory (HBM)is the fastest, most expensive, and most contested memory tier. Every byte spent on a redundant weight copy, an idle session’s KV cache, or a recomputed prefix is a byte that is not being used to produce tokens. The question is no longer how much memory a GPU has, but how much useful work each byte delivers. The generational data in Figure 1 below shows why. From GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin, capacity held at 288 GB while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s. agentic throughput per megawatt grew far faster. On SemiAnalysis AgentX , which replays recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps and growing context, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 then delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user. Figure 1. GPU throughput grew by 30x while HBM capacity remained approximately the same from GB300 NVL72 to Vera Rubin NVL72. Capacity alone cannot explain a 30x gain delivered from the same 288 GB per GPU. The difference is how much useful work each byte delivers. NVIDIA treats this as a co-design problem that spans GPU architecture, the scale-up interconnect, serving software, the CPU, and storage. This post examines five ways that co-design maximizes the value of each byte of memory, from the bits that encode a single weight to the shared storage that preserves and reuses context across agentic turns and nodes. 1. How does NVFP4 store more intelligence in fewer bytes? The most direct way to raise the value of a byte is to make each value smaller without losing what it encodes. NVFP4 does this with a 4-bit E2M1 element and two levels of scaling: Every 16-value micro-block shares an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, and a per-tensor FP32 scale sits on top. The result is a format that is small enough to free significant HBM, yet granular enough to preserve accuracy where naive 4-bit formats fall short. Figure 2. NVFP4 combines 4-bit values with block-level and tensor-level scaling. Applied to weights, NVFP4 reduces the model footprint by approximately 3.5x relative to FP16 and 1.8x relative to FP8, freeing memory for what agentic inference needs most: more KV-cache capacity, larger batches, and higher concurrency. NVFP4 has become the default precision for open agentic benchmarks with strict accuracy requirements, including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints. Across these benchmarks and leading mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, it delivers up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline at the same interactivity (Figure 3 below). Figure 3. NVFP4 delivers 4x the throughput per megawatt of FP8 at the same interactivity for DeepSeek R1 on GB300. The same principle extends to the KV cache itself. NVFP4 KV cache cuts the cache footprint by up to 50% compared with FP8, so approximately 2x more context stays resident on device. Fewer evictions mean higher cache-hit rates during prefill, while a smaller cache means less bandwidth consumed during decode. Figure 4. NVFP4 KV cache archives over 99% of BF16 baseline scores across 10 DeepSeek-v4-Pro benchmarks NVFP4 shrinks the bytes. The next question is where those bytes live, and how many copies of them the AI factory has to keep. 2. How does the NVLink scale-up domain turn 72 GPUs into one memory pool? MoE models activate only a subset of parameters per token, but every expert’s weights must still live somewhere in HBM. When experts are packed onto a small number of GPUs, each GPU spends a large share of its memory on weights, and each decode step pays a heavy weight-loading cost for the MoE GroupGEMMs. The bytes are resident, but they are not working hard. Wide expert parallelism (Wide-EP) in NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM changes that ratio by spreading experts across eight or more GPUs. With DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer, or 232 expert blocks across 58 MoE layers out of 14,848 in the full model. Fewer expert weights per GPU means: Capacity: More HBM per GPU is left for KV cache, larger batches, and higher concurrency. Arithmetic intensity: GroupGEMM kernels reuse each loaded weight across more tokens, raising FLOPs per byte. Balance: The Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB) redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes, so no GPU’s memory is overcommitted while another sits idle. Figure 5. GB300 NVL72 delivers 10x the token throughput per megawatt of H200 NVL8 at 100 tokens per second per user. This only works because the scale-up domain makes remote bytes nearly as useful as local ones. Every MoE layer triggers all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic, and without a high-bandwidth fabric, those collectives would erase the gains. On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs that traffic, and large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user. Vera Rubin NVL72 extends the same design point. Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, for roughly 20.7 TB of HBM4 across the rack. Rubin also adds inline memory tensor acceleratory (TMA) descriptor updates, so one shared descriptor can serve every expert with a common layout, reducing the metadata overhead that grows with expert count. Wide-EP decides where weight bytes live. The next lever decides whether KV cache bytes, once computed, are ever computed again. 3. How does NVIDIA Dynamo make every cached byte count? The key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens so the model can reuse them instead of recomputing them. This inference state is ephemeral and can be evicted and recomputed when needed, but KV cache is only valuable if it is reused. Agentic workloads are full of reuse opportunities: system prompts, tool schemas, shared documents, and the growing history of a multistep task. But if a request lands on a GPU that does not hold its prefix, or if that prefix was evicted moments earlier, the system pays for prefill again. The bytes existed; they were just in the wrong place. NVIDIA Dynamo is the distributed serving layer that closes this gap. It treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource rather than a per-GPU side effect, and it does so through three co-designed capabilities: KV-aware routing: The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing requests. It balances existing context against the cost of sending work to an utilized GPU and turns potential recomputations into cache hits. Disaggregated serving: Prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, each sized for its own compute and memory profile. Decode GPUs can dedicate HBM to KV cache and batch size rather than reserving headroom for bursty prefill. KV Cache Runner (KVCR): This tracks where every block lives across configured GPU, pinned CPU, and storage tiers, including local SSDs and mounted network filesystems. A prefix preserved outside HBM can be restored when a later request needs it, allowing useful context to survive GPU eviction and continue saving prefill work. KVCR uses the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) for its storage-transfer paths, allowing cached blocks to move while the GPU processes other work. KVCR also enables distributed reuse, with router-provided hints helping a selected worker retrieve cached context from a peer, while the inference engine retains control of GPU memory and local host offloading. The additional KVCR-Guard feature preserves committed KVCR-managed host-memory cache across an engine failure as long as the guard service and host remain available. Figure 6. Dynamo combines KV-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and tiered KV cache reuse. Dynamo’s KV-cache offloading depends on fast retrieval: Preserving a prefix outside HBM saves time when loading it is faster than repeating prefill. NIXL connects this offloading path to external storage systems.

title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call . Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”). The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs: Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy: The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel : your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity. Add Web Answer as a connector target. The connectorId tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer. Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE , the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until get_gateway_target reports the target status as READY before you call it. As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set parameterValues to {"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}} . Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s tools/list and calls it with tools/call , like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client. When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool ( web-answer-tool___WebAnswer ). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations. Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks. Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [ 1 ], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list: structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain. Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it: If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges. Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools: Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include: Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon. Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls. In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.

title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it. Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix. As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component. Figure 1: Block diagram of the VLM-based multi-model fusion approach, including VLM, OCR, and classifier models A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job rather than a foundation model fine-tuning run.
