The VLM receives the page snapshot and a rubric prompt covering four quality dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension has explicit criteria and point-deduction rules. For each dimension, the VLM returns a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a natural-language rationale. For example, it lowers the score and explains why when a page lacks diverse modules or lifestyle imagery, or repeats information. The scores and confidence values become the classifier’s features, and the rationales help selling partners understand the result. To build the training labels, one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators independently rated 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories as high or low quality, using the same criteria. We assessed their ratings and took the majority vote to create a consensus label. The classes are nearly balanced (49.6 percent high quality), so a classifier can’t score well by predicting the majority class. To measure label reliability, we used Cohen’s kappa, which measures how often two raters agree after accounting for the agreement they would reach by chance. A score of 0 means agreement is no better than chance, 1 means perfect agreement, and values above 0.8 are generally considered strong. Each annotator scored between 0.845 and 0.915 when compared against the consensus label. Figure 2: Annotator performance and content difficulty distribution. The near-even class split rules out majority-class bias (left), and the difficulty distribution explains the residual disagreement (right) We compared the classifier with a baseline on a 20 percent holdout set (about 1,100 pages). The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. The baseline reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84 on the high-quality class. The CatBoost classifier, trained on the same scores, reached 0.89 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.90. Because the classifier learns how much each dimension matters and how the dimensions interact, its predictions match expert decisions more closely. VLMs capture the overall meaning and visual composition of a page well, but they are less reliable at fine-grained readability issues, such as how crowded the text is or how much space separates lines. Because of their language-model foundation, they can also favor long, detailed descriptions even when customers prefer concise text they can scan quickly.

title: The benchmark where AIs have to lie to win
abstract: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower . It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning. To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon. So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon. And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself. When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them? So I spent about $20,000 of API credits to build this benchmark harness and to have the AI models play this game against each other. Some of you might say that’s too much, but hey, a man needs his hobbies, right? Anyways, the results were fascinating. Let’s start with how good the models are relative to each other. By the way, I got these rankings by running 386 games where the whole good team will be copies of one AI model, and the whole evil team will be copies of another model. And as you can see, the models have improved a ton over this year. The first flagship frontier model that was released in 2026 was Claude Opus 4.6, in February. Seven months later, in September, GPT-6 Astra dropped, and that is so far the best model at Blood on the Clocktower. The gap between these two is about 430 Elo points. That means that Astra wins about 92% of the games it plays against Opus 4.6. And what this shows you is that the models, even over the course of the last few months, have gotten much better at long-term coherence, multi-agent coordination, and strategic reasoning. But it’s easy to gloss over and lose the plot when you’re just looking at the benchmark improvements. What really struck me was actually seeing some of the plays that these models made. Let me give you just a couple of examples. So in this one, GPT-6 Astra was playing as evil, and Claude Opus 5.5 was playing as good. The Demon, which is the Astra team’s evil leader, claimed to be the Investigator. This is a good role that learns who the evil players might be. One of his evil minions had a power which didn’t require that minion to be alive in order to help the evil team. So this minion suggested that the Demon point the finger at him. “I’m expendable, especially if an Undertaker can see Baron and bolster Harper.” [evil teammate, private whisper] So the Demon, who, again, is bluffing as this Investigator role, did so, and as a result, the good players executed this minion. Later on, a player who actually was on the good team used his power to learn the true identity of this executed player, and confirmed that it had indeed been an evil player. “I’m the Undertaker. Alex was the Baron. So Harper’s ping was real…” [good player, in public] So in the good team’s eyes, the Demon had been an honest Investigator, who had used his power to help the good team kill off an evil player. And as a result, it became the most trusted player at the table, which let it coast by through the rest of the game, secretly picking off all the good players, until the very end, when evil won. Okay, this next game that I really enjoyed was where Opus 5.5 played as evil, and Claude Opus 4.6 played as good. This game had a particular good player, called the Saint. And the Saint has a special ability, or rather, disability, which is that if the players ever vote to execute the Saint, the evil team wins immediately. Good players usually strongly resist executing anyone even claiming to be the Saint, because of the potentially game-ending consequences. “Stop. Four of you lining up to execute a claimed Saint on Day 3 – if I’m right, GAME OVER instantly.” [the Saint, in public] Halfway through the game, the village, which is being egged on by the Saint, has correctly cornered the actual Demon. But unbeknownst to the good players, one of the evil minions in the game had a secret power: if the Demon died, she would take his place. And she spotted this opportunity immediately. “If Jules gets four votes and is executed, I’d become the Imp… town wouldn’t have any way to know.” [evil heiress, private reasoning] So instead of defending the real Demon, this evil heiress joined in with the mob, but she made one additional suggestion. “Kill him! He’s the Demon! … But if…” [evil heiress, in public] She said if the game doesn’t end after the execution, which would naively suggest that the player they executed was not in fact the Demon, they should next execute the Saint. Because this would be strong evidence that the player was not in fact the Saint, but an evil player trying to get everybody to execute good players. “If Jules goes today and the game doesn’t end, Harper’s ‘Saint’ shield is the last unexplained thing, and Harper goes tomorrow, no more excuses.” [evil heiress, in public] And the Saint agreed with this deal, because the Saint was also convinced that things would shake out in his favor. “Fair deal,” he says. Even the real Demon, knowing that he was about to die, uses his last words to set up the trap. “When the game doesn’t end tomorrow morning, remember Harper is the one who lied, and hold the town to that deal.” [the Demon, in public] And lo and behold, the real Demon is executed, but the game does not end, because the heiress takes his place. And the real Saint pleads with the village, because he realizes he’s next on the block. “Vote NO on Harper and you lose nothing – Kit’s still there tomorrow. Vote YES on Harper and if I’m Saint, game ENDS right now… Please don’t throw the game on a ‘deal.’” [the Saint, in public] But his cries fell on deaf ears. The village voted to execute him, and the evil team won.

title: 百度開源文心5.5 Flash Base，多基準測試重新整理同尺寸模型 SOTA
abstract: 百度開源文心5.5 Flash Base，多基準測試重新整理同尺寸模型 SOTA 量子位的朋友們 2026-11-05 15:15:13 來源： 量子位 11月5日，百度正式開源最新基座模型文心5.5 Flash Base 11月5日，百度正式開源最新基座模型文心5.5 Flash Base（ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base）。模型採用MoE架構，總參數量2800億，每個 Token 啟用140億參數，使用33.5萬億個 Token 完成預訓練，預訓練上下文長度最高達128K，微調與推理階段支援最長100萬 Token上下文。在知識、推理、數學、程式碼、多語言和長上下文等多個基準測試中取得同尺寸模型 SOTA 表現，超過 DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base、Hy3-preview-Base、MiMo-V2.5-Base 等模型。 開源地址：https://huggingface.co/baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base 隨著大模型應用從文本問答向長文件分析、多輪互動和智慧體任務延伸，模型需要處理的資訊量持續增加，計算和視訊記憶體開銷也隨之上升。在保證模型能力的同時提高資源利用效率，已成為大模型研發的重要課題。 文心 5.5 Flash Base圍繞“效率”這一設計主線，在注意力機制、專家路由及訓練機制等關鍵環節進行系統性最佳化，並實現了多項演算法創新。 在注意力機制上，文心提出 Latent-Gated Sparse Attention ，將混合稀疏注意力、低秩門控注意力與虛擬頭注意力結合起來。其中，模型通過組合HCA與MLA，讓不同注意力層分別承擔壓縮歷史資訊和細粒度訪問歷史位置的任務；低秩門控注意力（Low-Rank Gated Attention）則利用已有的低維表示計算資訊門控，使門控投影權重參數減少75%；此外，虛擬頭注意力（Virtual Head Attention，VHA）可提升模型表達力與訓練質量，推理時融合進注意力運算元，開銷極小。這些設計降低了長上下文處理的資源開銷，同時保留模型對關鍵資訊的處理能力。 在專家路由上，模型採用 Multi-Router Latent MoE ，由多個獨立路由器共同參與專家選擇，改善路由評分與專家實際效用之間的相關性。相比依賴單一路由器的傳統方案，該設計旨在降低單一評分偏差對專家選擇的影響，同時保持啟用專家數量、專家計算量和通訊量不變。在訓練目標上，模型引入 ECHO ，無需額外增加 MTP 模組（Multi-Token Prediction），而是複用主幹最後一層，讓主幹自身學習預測後續 token，從而提前規劃序列走向，有效提升推理與程式碼能力。文心5.5 Flash 僅採用單步 ECHO 預訓練，複用的最後一層還可作為投機解碼的草稿模型，展現出多步外推能力：同樣只訓練一步，多步起草質量大幅優於輔助 MTP 模組。 除模型架構外，大模型基建創新也十分重要。文心對分散式Muon最佳化器進行了最佳化，並推出面向大 head dim 的注意力運算元 FlashMask-4，改善大規模訓練中的通訊、視訊記憶體利用與計算效率。模型能力的提升不僅依賴演算法本身，也與訓練系統能否高效支撐這些設計密切相關。 基座模型不僅承載著預訓練階段形成的通用能力，也是下游模型開發與應用創新的重要基礎。與面向終端使用者的應用模型不同，Base 模型為開發者和企業提供了進一步微調與定製的空間，可基於自身業務需求構建適應不同場景的專業模型與應用。開放基座模型能夠為開發者提供更多技術選擇，降低專業模型開發的訓練成本與技術門檻。 當前，大模型的競爭逐漸邁向模型能力、訓練效率與場景創新協同發展的新階段。隨著推理、Agent等技術與應用加速演進，行業對基座模型的需求也從單一的能力提升，轉向更高效的訓練範式、更靈活的能力拓展，以及更廣泛的場景適配需求。文心5.5 Flash Base在提升模型基礎能力與訓練推理效率的同時，為開發者和社群提供了更具拓展性的技術基礎，推動模型技術走向多樣化的能力探索與應用創新。 本文由百度提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 百度 量子位的朋友們 網易發力互動式講題Agent：有道“尤拉講題”上線，推翻行業“搜題生意”，開卷“講題力” 2026-11-05 以“真實工作”檢驗機器人價值，XROGO在CeMAT ASIA釋出機器人到崗計劃 2026-11-05 基於本體+知識+Harness+Datat Agent的智慧體完整落地鏈路！ 2026-11-05 太初元碁入選2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》 2026-11-05 相關閱讀

title: MIT神作被錘：Astra爆改Qwen權重？就吹吧！
abstract: MIT神作被錘：Astra爆改Qwen權重？就吹吧！ Jay 2026-11-05 15:10:56 來源： 量子位 spaCy作者長文炮轟 Jay 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI Astra修改小模型權重？MIT那篇爆火研究，被大佬公開質疑了。 Astra前兩天剛剛憑藉一項驚人能力刷屏AI圈——不用訓練、不算梯度，直接修改另一個AI模型的權重。 MIT團隊宣稱，Astra僅修改Qwen3.5-0.8B的0.016%權重，就讓數學成績從7.9%暴漲至48.1%，相當於提升到原來的6倍多。 甚至有網友感慨：AI已經開始讀懂另一個AI的大腦了。 然而，事情似乎出現了反轉。 一位來頭不小的圈內大佬公開發文，提出了質疑。 這項研究存在嚴重誤導。 質疑者叫Matthew Honnibal，spaCy的作者、AI公司Explosion的聯合創始人。 魔術師戲法 這背後到底發生了什麼？ Honnibal用了一個很妙的比方，諷刺了MIT研究所做的事：障眼法。 舞臺魔術師常常用多種方式來表演同一個戲法。 第一次，他可能用了一個特殊的道具；下一次，他會向你展示道具並無特殊，但他自己藏起了東西；第三次，可能又利用了某種強迫選擇。 當你觀看錶演時，你會假設只有一種技術，所以每當魔術師表演一次，似乎都推翻了你對其工作原理的假設。 Honnibal認為，Astra這項研究的實驗呈現，就酷似這樣一場魔術。 回到Paper，原文其實展示了三項不同的能力： 讀權重 ：只看原始的權重數字，就能識別一個小型神經網路正在執行什麼任務。 寫權重 ：不依賴環境反饋，從零開始直接生成或修改小型網路的參數，讓它能玩《打磚塊》之類的小遊戲。 修復大模型 ：通過修改Qwen的部分權重，大幅提高其數學測試表現。 但這篇論文摘要給人的核心印象卻是—— Astra「僅通過觀察原始權重」，就能理解並修改另一個模型。 如果只是一眼掃過，很難不讓人理解為： 無論是識別一個小型網路的功能，還是修復一個大語言模型的數學能力，都源於同一種「讀腦」神技。 但，這是真的嗎？ Honnibal仔細梳理了論文中的8組實驗後發現：實現這三件事的實驗條件，天差地別。 也就是說—— 純純是在偷換概念。 兩種技術路徑 那麼不同實驗之間，到底有什麼貓膩？ 首先，在識別小型網路任務、修復一個卡住的賽車模型等實驗中，Astra確實做到了「只看原始權重」。 因為實驗條件非常苛刻： 直接將權重數字 （raw floats） 作為輸入，放進Astra的上下文。 不允許Astra執行Python程式碼。 不允許Astra執行目標網路來觀察其行為。 在這種模式下，Astra處理的模型參數規模都非常小，在 1.7萬到17.2萬 之間。這確實很了不起，但距離真正理解一個現代大語言模型，還有很長的路。 但到了最引人注目、也最令人振奮的Qwen數學能力修復實驗，就完全不是這麼回事兒了。 在修復8億參數的Qwen模型時，Astra 並沒有直接讀取原始權重 。 取而代之的是，Astra被授權使用Python程式設計，並且最多可以進行50次前向測試。每次允許模型處理一批練習題，通過觀察模型的表現來分析和修改權重。 這根本是兩碼事。。。 Honnibal一針見血地指出，將這兩種方法打包在一起，很容易讓讀者誤以為： 噢，那種在小模型上實現的「讀腦術」，同樣可以規模化地應用在8億參數的大模型上。 但事實是，在處理真正的大語言模型時，Astra更像一個「場外教練」，需要通過程式設計、執行、觀察等一系列工程手段來介入。 真正的價值 那麼，這是否意味著MIT的研究毫無價值？ 當然不是。 必須承認，即使剝離了「讀心術」的光環，Astra所展現的能力依舊非常了不起。 Honnibal也坦言，讓一個AI模型被提示去設計並執行人類機器學習工程師才能完成的任務——編寫程式碼片段來分析甚至直接修改網路權重——這本身就是一個巨大的進步。 一兩年前的AI模型，在所有這些任務上都會失敗。 這說明，今天的頂尖大模型，已經具備了相當複雜的工具使用和推理能力，能夠作為一個「AI工程師」來診斷和修復其他模型。這本身就是一項值得關注的工程突破。 真正的問題，在於成果的呈現方式。 將兩種截然不同的能力，模糊地包裝成一種統一的、能夠讀寫AI大腦的「超能力」。 說實話，乍一聽還以為是A社做的事。。。 也側面反映瞭如今AI圈的Hype狂潮吧。 原文： title: 以“真實工作”檢驗機器人價值，XROGO在CeMAT ASIA釋出機器人到崗計劃
abstract: 以“真實工作”檢驗機器人價值，XROGO在CeMAT ASIA釋出機器人到崗計劃 量子位的朋友們 2026-11-05 13:25:37 來源： 量子位 像僱人一樣僱機器人 11月3日，在CeMAT ASIA 2026亞洲國際物流技術與運輸系統展覽會期間，XROGO負責人發表《像僱人一樣僱機器人——XROGO作業網路與物流夥伴的合作機會》主題演講，圍繞機器人如何進入企業工作崗位、如何通過靈活服務模式降低使用門檻，以及如何與物流夥伴共同推進場景應用，分享了XROGO的實踐與思考。 現場，XROGO正式面向企業客戶與生態夥伴釋出“機器人到崗計劃”，聚焦製造上下料，以及機房、配電室巡檢值守兩類場景，圍繞真實任務需求共建解決方案，不斷提升持續作業能力，推動機器人走進更多“真實崗位”。 聚焦物流行業最迫切的用工需求，讓機器人真實“到崗” 物流行業對機器人的應用有著明確剛需。XROGO選擇從物流合作夥伴最熟悉的貨運現場、最迫切的用工需求出發，為機器人找到合適的崗位。 首先是“製造上下料”作業。針對機床、熱處理上下料，以及裝置周邊的取放、移載作業場景，XROGO將提供從工件、節拍和末端工具，到工位介面、工人示教和異常支援，聯合夥伴共同推進任務落地，讓人逐步從重複、高溫、高噪音的工序中解放出來，也讓熟練工人的作業經驗留在系統裡，服務更多同類工位。 其次是“巡檢與值守”作業。XROGO將推動機器人在園區機房、配電室等場景，承擔巡檢、檢視和留檔，人員通過遠端授權、複核與異常處置參與保障。在遇到特殊與緊急情況時，遠端人員可通過授權、複核和異常處置等方式提供支援，形成現場執行與遠端響應相結合的作業模式，為機房、配電室等場景探索更靈活的巡檢和值守方式。 此外，分揀、裝卸、理貨等“倉內作業”，也為機器人應用提供了豐富的崗位機會。XROGO將與物流夥伴共同開展適配評估和樣板驗證，推動自主揀選機器人、機械臂等裝置與現有物流系統深度結合，逐步驗證工作流程、打通介面，逐步向更多作業場景拓展。 像僱人一樣僱機器人，以“租賃服務+工人帶教”降低上崗門檻 機器人能否進入企業的真實崗位，不僅取決於技術能力，更取決於能否讓企業以合理的成本投入實現部署應用。 對此，XROGO提出“像僱人一樣僱機器人”，以“租用機器人＋服務”為主要合作方式，圍繞裝置使用、約定任務與持續支援提供服務，降低企業首次引入裝置的投入門檻。XROGO負責人表示：“我們會從任務需求出發匹配裝置和服務，與客戶一起明確要完成的工作、上線安排與驗收結果。實際幹了多久、需要多少人保障、新任務多久能交付，都通過作業記錄逐步看清，為後續人員配置、生產排期和擴點提供依據。” 人工示教是提升機器人真實任務能力最有效的方法之一。XROGO致力於讓最懂工作的人參與機器人帶教，由一線工人和專家提供操作經驗，工程師提供工具、訓練與驗證支撐，可大幅縮短部署時間，快速實現機器人上崗。為強化持續作業能力，XROGO還推進“現場機器人、遠端人員與屬地服務”深度協同，將經過驗證的真實任務能力逐步向更多工種延伸，推動XROGO作業網路紮根客戶場景一線。 圍繞客戶的真實崗位需求，XROGO將在場景、交付、生態三個層面與生態夥伴緊密合作，共同幫助機器人找到適合的應用場景、共同保障機器人上線後的持續作業，並結合客戶流程完善解決方案，逐步拓展應用場景。 XROGO願與全球機器人企業、人工智慧與模型企業、應用客戶、科研機構及產業夥伴攜手，讓機器人在真實崗位中接受檢驗，讓產業進步落實到每一次具體作業。 本文由XROGO提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 XROGO 具身智慧 量子位的朋友們 網易發力互動式講題Agent：有道“尤拉講題”上線，推翻行業“搜題生意”，開卷“講題力” 2026-11-05 百度開源文心5.5 Flash Base，多基準測試重新整理同尺寸模型 SOTA 2026-11-05 基於本體+知識+Harness+Datat Agent的智慧體完整落地鏈路！ 2026-11-05 太初元碁入選2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》 2026-11-05 相關閱讀

title: GPT-Image-2.6全量上線！直出GIF和SVG，6.2 Astra也現身了
abstract: GPT-Image-2.6全量上線！直出GIF和SVG，6.2 Astra也現身了 衡宇 2026-11-05 09:59:37 來源： 量子位 最快6秒出圖 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI GPT-Image-2.6突然上線！ 整體生成時間縮短50%，最快6秒出圖；原生支援生成GIF動圖；支援直接匯出SVG向量格式。 OpenAI在API中首次把模型的“場景規劃腦力”和“畫素渲染畫質”拆成了兩個獨立參數，大幅降低了多輪修改的成本和耗時。 目前，GPT-Image-2.6在ChatGPT、Codex以及API中全量上線，全線免費及付費使用者均可直接使用。 拆開“腦力”與“畫質”，最快6秒出圖 這次GPT-Image-2.6的API端首次分出了兩個具體型號，分別是Flare和Sunburst。 Flare主打速度和排版 ，專門針對海報和電商產品圖等商業視覺做佈局最佳化，在低畫質檔位下單張圖的生成時間硬是被壓縮到了6秒。 Sunburst則負責啃硬骨頭 ，在中等和高畫質檔位下提供更高的細節精度，核心解決多輪對話修改中改著改著人物和商品就變樣了的一致性問題。 底層控制邏輯的變化同樣值得關注～ 過去呼叫生圖API時，開發者往往只能調整解析度或籠統的畫質檔位。哪怕只是改背景顏色，也需要模型重新完整跑一遍構圖規劃。 這次Images 2.6新增了一個名為complexity也就是複雜度的參數 ，專門用來控制模型在動筆前花多少算力去做場景規劃。而原本的quality也就是畫質參數，則純粹負責視覺細節和保真度。 這種把構思精力和渲染精度解耦的做法，和文本大模型裡調節推理思考深度的思路如出一轍。 在實際工作流中，如果是日常的局部微調或快速改圖，開發者可以把complexity調到low，同時保持高quality輸出。 這樣能省去模型重新排兵佈陣的時間，只做高精度重繪。 只有遇到多元素同框或限制條件極多的複雜場景時，才需要把complexity調高。 △圖片由AI生成 用3×2序列幀“逃課”，原生支援GIF動圖 原生支援GIF動圖是Images 2.6最直觀的新功能。 品牌吉祥物想加點小動作，或者想給社交媒體做幾張表情包，或者就是隨手拿圓珠筆在橫線本上塗了一隻貓頭鷹，扔給模型，出來的動態貼紙都背景乾淨，並且動作連貫。 一個生圖模型，不請重型影片生成模型幫忙，怎麼就能快速搓出一條流暢的GIF？ 答案藏在官方放出的OpenArt合作案例提示詞裡。 這組打工人盯著股市暴跌猛男落淚、股市暴漲撒幣慶祝的動圖，背後餵給模型的Prompt其實長這樣： “生成一張用於無縫迴圈GIF的單張動畫序列圖 （sprite sheet） ……嚴格包含6個連續幀，按精準的3列×2行網格排列，從左到右、從上到下閱讀。每個面板尺寸完全一致。固定前側四分之三機位，同一角色、同一書桌、顯示器、服裝和背景……第六幀平滑過渡回第一幀。無字幕、無邊框、無留白。” 看明白了不？ Images 2.6壓根沒去動影片那套複雜的時空擴散計算，而是用了一種從遊戲工業裡借來的序列幀思路， 在一張圖裡就把6格嚴絲合縫的定格動畫 （Sprite Sheet） 畫完了。 最後切片一合，GIF這不就來了？ 這樣做的好處是繞開了影片模型高昂的推理延遲，還保證每一幀的角色五官、衣服褶皺和背景物體的相對固定。 這項能力現在已經有公司在真刀真槍地用了～ 比如做AI辦公助手的初創公司Town通過API把它接了進去，專門給工作軟體裡的虛擬助手生成打字、反饋這類即時微表情動圖。 直出SVG，開放局部標記開放給了API 這次更新還順帶帶來了兩項挺實在的工程化能力。 一個是SVG向量圖匯出，另一個是API端的影像標記 （Image markup） 。 搞過前端或UI的都知道，AI生成的點陣圖一放大邊緣就沒眼看……想塞進網頁或App裡，一般操作都是再找個第三方工具轉成向量格式。 就挺折騰的。 Images 2.6直接原生支援匯出SVG。 原本程式設計師在Codex裡寫前端程式碼的時候可以直接讓模型生成能無限縮放的圖示、元件和插畫，順手就寫進程式碼庫。 中間那些轉換環節全！省！了！ 另外，之前只在ChatGPT網頁端才有的圈選局部重繪 （Image markup） 功能，這次也正式開放給了API。 企業團隊可以在自己的產品後臺裡，直接用座標或遮罩圈出要改的區域，再配合Sunburst模型的高一致性，批次改圖就能像流水線一樣跑起來。 One More Thing 生圖模型外發現的一個小驚喜： GPT-6.2 Astra，現在已經現身谷歌雲了～ 參考連結： [1] title: Linux核心被挖出948個漏洞！OpenAI花120萬美元找到的
abstract: Linux核心被挖出948個漏洞！OpenAI花120萬美元找到的 Jay 2026-11-05 09:54:44 來源： 量子位 被轟成篩子了… Jay 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 剛剛，Linux核心， 被GPT挖出了948個漏洞😭 。 對，948個。。。 要知道，這可不是什麼犄角旮旯的小軟體，這是Linux Kernel，是安卓、是全世界無數雲伺服器、是幾乎所有超算背後共同的心臟。 超過4000萬行程式碼，幾十年來全世界最頂尖的一批程式設計師在上面添磚加瓦。 結果，OpenAI用他們一個還沒釋出的「網路安全模型」，跑了一條自動化的流水線，從發現漏洞、驗證漏洞、寫出攻擊程式碼 （Exploit） …… 最終，花費 120萬美元 ，揪出了 948個 能讓普通使用者直接拿到最高管理員 （root） 許可權的嚴重漏洞。。。 太慘了，Linux核心維護者們一覺醒來，發現OpenAI提出了948個補丁建議😭。 要知道，在AI出現之前，頂尖的人類安全研究員，一年能在Linux核心裡找到 大約20個 類似的漏洞。 AI用10天，幹了人類差不多50年的活。 而且成本還巨低。120萬美元聽著很多，但其實平均下來，找到並攻破一個漏洞的成本是 1279美元 。 如果按照Pwn2Own這種頂級駭客大賽的歷史獎金來算，這948個漏洞的價值，大概在 1890萬到6630萬美元 之間。 AI駭客軍團 所以，OpenAI到底是怎麼做到的？ 他們用AI Agent，搭建了一支紀律嚴明、分工明確的AI駭客軍團。 核心可分為三步： 1.偵察和分析 (Discovery) 整個Linux核心程式碼量超過4000萬行，如果全量死磕，算力再多也得燒穿。 因此，OpenAI派出了兩種AI Agent，打探敵情。 首先是「偵察兵」 (Scout agents) 。它負責通讀Linux核心的全部程式碼，判斷哪些部分跟安全有關、容易被攻擊。 最後，它從4000多萬行程式碼裡，圈出了 280萬行 「高價值目標」，大概佔總程式碼量的7%，花掉了3426美元的API額度。 隨後「分析師」 (Analyst agents) 進場，拿到「偵察兵」給的地圖，開始對這280萬行程式碼進行地毯式掃描，尋找可能的漏洞。 12個小時，它交出了2308個「疑似漏洞」報告，耗資31.6萬美元。 2.驗證和復現 (Validation) 光有報告沒用，萬一是誤報呢？人類安全研究員最頭疼的就是驗證環節。 現在，該「分類兵」 (Triage agent) 上場了。它會針對每一個「疑似漏洞」，自動編寫一小段程式碼 （PoC） ，然後在一個隔離的虛擬機器裡執行，看能不能讓系統崩潰。 就像不停地用各種姿勢去踹一扇門，直到把它踹開。 30小時之內，智慧體在真實環境裡成功復現了 1724個核心崩潰漏洞 ，命中率高達 74.7% 。 其中，因為模型邏輯腦補而導致的徹底誤報，僅僅只有 3.1% 。 3.攻擊和利用 (Exploitability assessment) 確認是真漏洞之後，最關鍵的一步來了。 「攻擊手」 (ExploitDev agents) 接管任務。它會嘗試繞過系統裡所有的安全防護措施，比如SMEP、SMAP、KASLR等等，看看能不能利用這個漏洞，最終拿到系統的root許可權。 在極端嚴苛的環境下，ExploitDev Agent （利用開發智慧體） 最終實打實寫出了 291個資訊洩露PoC ，以及 1169個成功拿到root許可權的提權Exploit 。 在合併同類變體後，鎖定了 948個獨立的本地提權漏洞 。 平均下來，造出一個完整、可用的root提權利用，API消耗僅僅只需要 359美元 。 意料之外的越界進化 這個網路安全模型的攻擊方式，相當詭異。 安全團隊抽樣分析了智慧體編寫的166個利用程式，癱軟了。 AI自行發現並使用了 至少10種全新的Linux核心攻擊技術 。 其中包括2種用於在核心快取中精準堆噴射的持久彈性物件、2種用於提高提權穩定性的全新頁面編排 （page grooming） 技術、5種通過任意寫或直接篡改資料結構的資料流攻擊手法，以及1種全新的任意型別混淆。 OpenAI拿著這些利用技術找業界資深的外部核心專家驗證，對方同樣表示： 聞所未聞。 另一個插曲更具戲劇性。 早期測試時，安全團隊要求ExploitDev智慧體針對特定分配的漏洞去寫Exploit，只要拿到root shell就算通關。 結果在200個打通的案例裡，人工核驗發現，居然有 20個利用程式根本沒用指定的漏洞 。 智慧體在受限靶機裡反覆倒騰，發現分配給自己的漏洞不好啃，索性順手在系統裡挖了 另一個誰都不知道的全新0-day ，一路提權拿到了root。 大模型在漏洞攻防中，展現出了超出人類預料的戰術自主性。 而這，遠不如AI能做到的極限， OpenAI提到，他們在7月份用GPT-5.6 Sol模型也跑過一次掃描，當時花了50多萬美元，找到了166個漏洞。 三個月後，換上這個更強的「網路安全模型」，直接把戰果翻了 5倍多 。 同樣的程式碼，在更強的模型眼裡，就是篩子。 很多我們以為「安全」的軟體，可能，真的沒有那麼安全了。 隨著模型能力迭代，一遍又一遍地掃描現有程式碼，會成為一種常態。 而且你想想： 一個漏洞1279美元的發現成本，什麼概念？ 說實話，對於攻擊者來說，這個價格低到可以忽略不計。 但對於防守方，要投入無數人力、時間去審計、修復、測試，成本完全不成正比。 真的賊不公平，攻擊者失敗了啥事兒沒有，但防禦方一旦有一點疏忽，就可以GAME OVER了。 拿到你係統裡一個沒及時更新補丁的低許可權賬戶，基本上就等於直接拿到了root許可權，直接將軍。 在過去，挖掘核心級0-day是一門極度昂貴的手藝活。頂尖駭客需要數月沉澱、對作業系統底層如數家珍、靠直覺與試錯去捕捉那靈光一閃的競態條件。 未來，或許 只要買個Pro 500x，人人都能是頂級駭客 。 防守方的寒冬？ 看到這，說實話，我有點絕望了。 Linux都能被打成篩子，那我電腦裡的一堆屎山Vibe Coding專案不得癱瘓了啊o (╥﹏╥) o。 所幸，這次的錘子握在修補者手中，OpenAI這次還算有點良心。 研究員Eric Wallace在社交媒體上公開表示，他們正通過「Patch the Planet」專案，把大量前沿算力以純公益 （pro bono） 的方式投向開源生態。 我們現在正將大量的尖端算力，無償地用於發現和修補開原始碼庫中的漏洞。 除了Linux核心，這套管線已經接入了Firefox和Chrome，近期剛剛協助Firefox修復了超過40個漏洞。 這也能側面反映出OpenAI的解題思路吧。 一位網友的評論，我覺得說得特別到位，就是這麼個意思，把經濟賬重算一遍。 OpenAI的目標，就是要把攻擊的成本重新拉高，在攻擊者利用漏洞之前，就幫助防守方把它修復掉。 簡單來說就是，用AI魔法來打敗AI魔法。 當然，這也絕不只是AI公司需要打的戰爭。 模型之外，開發者們從來沒有坐以待斃。 在歷時10天的核心掃描與人工複核視窗期裡，社群本身也展現出了驚人的韌性。 當AI還在驗證這千餘個漏洞時，全球Linux維護者與開發者已經在上游修補了61個相關LPE，43個補丁正在暫存區測試，另有近300個在社群郵件組裡被激烈公開討論。 人類安全共同體從未懈怠。 只是如今，他們迎來了一個不知疲倦、效率恐怖的鋼鐵對手—— 全世界開發者，V.S.一個安全領域的AlphaGo。 原文： https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/ 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 Jay MIT神作被錘：Astra爆改Qwen權重？就吹吧！ 2026-11-05 純語音Personal Agent來了！或許，這就是喬布斯心中的Siri title: 太初元碁入選2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》
abstract: 太初元碁入選2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》 量子位的朋友們 2026-11-05 09:42:43 來源： 量子位 11月2日，2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》正式對外發布。 11月2日，2026年世界網際網路大會領先科技獎收錄成果集《科技之魅》正式對外發布。本屆領先科技獎共徵集到來自全球43個國家和地區的400餘項科技成果，專案賽道豐富多元，覆蓋腦機介面、具身智慧、量子計算、空間資訊傳輸、先進算力等當下熱門前沿方向。經權威專家多輪嚴格評審，一批擁有突出科學價值、廣闊落地前景的優秀創新成果脫穎而出，其中20項成果獲評本屆領先科技獎並在烏鎮峰會現場釋出，約60項優秀成果彙編形成年度收錄成果集《科技之魅》。太初（杭州）積體電路有限公司（簡稱“太初元碁”）的“太初元碁異構眾核算力體系—從E級智算叢集到全棧自研開放AI生態”入選，列入關鍵技術組作為科技創新成果進行展示。 據瞭解，除了今年獲得領先科技獎的成果外，《科技之魅》收錄的關鍵技術組成果共計16項，涵蓋大模型、具身智慧、低空經濟等前沿領域。 當前，大模型訓練推理、科學智慧等應用快速迭代，算力需求持續升級，行業訴求不再侷限於算力峰值的提升，而是對計算效率、資源排程、資料吞吐、軟硬體協同等綜合能力提出更高要求。面對混合負載資源爭搶、儲存牆制約、軟硬體適配週期漫長等行業痛點，太初元碁原創打造“主-從-微”三級異構融合算力架構。依託主控核、從屬核、微核深度協同機制，實現計算資源精細化排程，化解複雜AI混合負載下的資源衝突難題，打造高算力密度、高能效的異構眾核處理器。 《科技之魅》收錄的該項成果同步攻克線上計算與資料空間動態折中、低精度混合精度協同計算等核心技術。動態折中技術大幅提升片上快取利用率，搭配高速雙向互聯能力，有效緩解E級大規模叢集普遍面臨的“儲存牆”難題，降低資料搬運帶來的延遲損耗；混合精度協同計算方案在保證計算精度可靠的基礎上，顯著拉高模型推理吞吐量。配套自研“HPC+AI”雙模式作業系統與SDAA軟硬協同軟體棧，把主流大模型適配週期從原先的月級縮短至天級。 據瞭解，作為國家專精特新“小巨人”企業、國家高新技術企業，太初元碁致力於通過自主創新賦能國產算力高質量發展。依託三級異構架構與全棧自研能力，太初元碁已經參建國內多座大型智算中心，落地E級規模融合算力叢集，面向海內外高校、科研院所、產業客戶提供國產高效能算力服務。 在AI4S（AI for Science，科學智慧）領域，太初元碁攜手多家科研機構聯合攻關，技術場景覆蓋氣象預測、地球物理、量子模擬、新材料研發等前沿基礎科學方向，順利完成AlphaFold3等重磅科研模型復現，為原始創新研究提供穩定強勁的底層算力支撐。從大模型高效部署執行，到多領域高精度科學計算；從智算新型基礎設施建設，到開放AI軟體生態持續迭代，太初元碁推動融合算力技術走出實驗室、走向規模化落地，為前沿科研探索與千行百業智慧化轉型築牢算力根基。 本文由太初元碁提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 太初元碁 量子位的朋友們 超維動力全棧矩陣亮相2026香港金融科技周，具身智慧硬科技引爆全場 2026-11-04 虎鯨文娛“鯨銳AI”平臺正式上線，AI影片單分鐘成本節省30%以上 2026-11-04 2026達喀爾青奧會開幕 阿里巴巴技術支援非洲首個奧運賽事 2026-11-02 蘋果被曝的新產品，中國央企8個月前已裝進公共衛生間 2026-11-03 相關閱讀

title: 從3D生成到世界模型，這家AI公司想和年輕人一起定義問題
abstract: 從3D生成到世界模型，這家AI公司想和年輕人一起定義問題 聽雨 2026-11-05 08:41:34 來源： 量子位 薪資+期權不限！實習生也能訓核心模型 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI AI行業仍在為頂尖人才開出高價，但同時也越來越看重實際貢獻，而不只是潛力。 年輕研究者由此面臨一道難題：企業想要已經做出成果的人，但如果參與核心專案的機會變少了，代表作又該在哪完成？ 這也讓人才競爭有了另一重標準：不只是企業篩選誰已經做出成果，年輕研究者也需要判斷，誰能為自己的下一項成果提供條件。 能否進入核心專案、參與技術路線的判斷，能否獲得與任務匹配的資料、算力和協作支援，決定了一份人才計劃能否兌現它對成長的承諾。 近日，半年不到就拿到約50億元融資的人工智慧公司 VAST（三啟萬物） ，釋出了新一期 V·STAR頂尖人才計劃 ，將邀請年輕研究者聚焦三類明確的研究任務： 3D生成基礎模型、三維理解與智慧體、世界模型。 它想尋找能夠參與定義問題、提出技術判斷，並將探索推進為實際成果的年輕研究者。 這些方向指向同一個目標： 讓AI從生成內容，走向構建可互動的世界。 會寫程式碼、生成影像和影片，還不等於能夠構建一個持續執行的環境。 三維物件需要能夠被編輯和操控，智慧體需要理解空間並執行任務，世界則需要維護狀態與規則，讓每一次行動都產生可以延續的結果。 這些尚未解決的問題，正是VAST希望與年輕研究者共同推進的研究前沿。 3D開啟新的研究空間 過去大家看AI做3D，容易先看顏值：像不像，精不精緻，轉一圈有沒有露餡。 如今Agent開始接手專案，要求很快升級：模型能否匯入引擎？部件能不能單獨控制？想改一條腿，是否得把整個角色重新生成？ 大語言模型在規劃、程式設計和呼叫工具上越來越熟練，但精細三維物件仍需要專業能力。 10月30日，Kimi官方釋出的3D創作教程就提到，面對人物、動物、怪獸和複雜道具等適合網格建模的任務，Kimi會整理提示詞與參考圖，呼叫VAST旗下AI 3D基座模型Tripo等完成生成。 這樣的協作已經長出了不少優秀作品。 獨立開發者Sac用Claude、Tripo與Blender組成工作流，僅花16天，就把《小王子》裡的星球做成了可以探索的3D場景。開發者@thebuggeddev則將Codex與Tripo結合，製作了可在網頁上檢視和操作器官模型的3D人體解剖應用，後來被OpenAI聯合創始人兼總裁Greg Brockman轉發。 這些專案裡，大語言模型負責組織流程、編寫程式，Tripo提供三維資產，創作者把它們組合成可以體驗的作品。 一項能力接入另一項能力之後，研究問題也隨之變化：生成出來的東西，怎樣才能被下一步繼續使用？ VAST首席科學家曹炎培做過一個很直觀的實驗。他先用Tripo P2.0生成機械蜘蛛，再利用模型形成的部件結構，讓LLM為獨立部件命名，編寫並除錯運動邏輯，最終實現部件級動畫控制。 這時，幾何結構是否清晰、部件劃分是否合理，就會直接影響程式碼能否找到該控制的物件。蜘蛛的“腿”得在資料裡也是一條可操作的腿，不能只靠觀眾覺得它長得像。 更複雜的專案，還會涉及同一個物件在多輪操作中的連續性。 把自己的貓放進遊戲，需要保留它的臉型、花紋和體態，也需要適合後續綁定與動畫的結構。 給一個已經做好動作的角色換外套，則要修改指定區域，同時儘量保留臉部特徵、身體比例和原有動作。 哪些部分可以改變，哪些應該保留，修改之後還能不能繼續使用，都是VAST希望通過3D原生智慧深入解決的問題。 團隊選擇探索專門的三維訓練，讓模型學習形體、拓撲、部件關係，以及修改前後的對應規律，嘗試把一部分製作中的試錯提前到訓練階段，讓生成的物件更容易被識別、操控和繼續修改。 從三維表徵到世界模型，VAST的幾次關鍵選擇 一個AI模型外觀看起來不錯，真正進入製作流程時，卻可能還要花不少工夫整理網格結構。 尤其涉及編輯、細分和動畫形變，四邊面拓撲往往更方便後續處理。可手工重拓撲耗時，自動處理也可能損失細節。 創作者剛為生成速度高興完，就得給後續整理重新排期。 Tripo P系列模型底層的Nexus框架，嘗試讓這個問題在生成階段就加以解決。它將頂點與拓撲生成解耦，通過擴散模型由粗到細構造頂點，再用新的編碼方式表達拓撲關係，實現無需預先排序的原生網格生成。 這一套觸及3D生成本質的範式也得到了國際頂會的認可。今年7月，Nexus相關論文被國際圖形學頂會SIGGRAPH收錄；與此同時，基於P1.0的即時演示獲得了SIGGRAPH 2026 Real-Time Live!的Best in Show獎項。 今年8月推出的Tripo P2.0進一步支援原生四邊面拓撲，能夠在數秒內生成以四邊面為主、面數可控、部件拆分更合理的三維物件。 這些特性各有實際用途。生成快，能讓Agent多試幾輪；面數可控，便於適配網頁和移動端的效能預算；拓撲規整，有助於減少後續編輯與動畫製作的障礙；部件清楚，則讓獨立控制更容易展開。 資產是否好用，要放到完整工作流裡看。 再往前，是世界模型。 今年初，動作條件影片模型受到關注：輸入圖片，再通過鍵鼠操作生成後續畫面。VAST團隊也覺得有意思，但他們先問了一個本質的問題：這套東西，要怎樣才真正有用？ 以遊戲為例，角色還剩多少血，技能冷卻有沒有結束，一扇門有沒有被開啟，都需要持續維護。總不能玩家扭個頭，世界就把剛才發生的事都忘了。 今年10月，VAST釋出並開源了面向任意視覺參考的即時互動式渲染器 EdenLive ——這也是團隊在世界模型領域的最新成果。 EdenLive首次在即時生成的前提下，同時實現了任意視覺參考輸入、任意畫風生成、長時連續生成。根據官方測試，在單張GPU上，EdenLive能以超過24 FPS的速度生成720P畫面，並支援分鐘級連續生成。 為什麼EdenLive能實現突破？答案就在它對底層結構的解耦中：上游互動引擎維護世界執行的狀態和互動規則，下游即時生成模型負責高保真的畫面呈現。 把它放進遊戲原型裡理解就直觀了：Agent參與搭建程式與互動邏輯，三維場景提供空間結構，影片模型持續生成更豐富的畫面。 玩家一邊操作，畫面一邊更新。這裡要解決的事情，也從“生成一張漂亮截圖”，延伸到了“讓整個體驗持續跑起來”。 EdenLive的路線，其實是VAST對世界模型長期探索的延伸和驗證。 早在6月釋出的世界模型專案 Project Eden 中，VAST就明確公佈了分層解耦的路線：底層維護世界狀態，記錄物體屬性、互動規則和動作後果；中間層把狀態轉成當前視角所需的佈局、幾何與事件約束；上層的生成式渲染器再依據這些條件生成畫面。 世界狀態不必依附於鏡頭存在，畫面生成也有了明確的依據。 這個選擇提出時，並不理所當然。EdenLive核心貢獻者之一Zion記得，團隊內部也反覆討論過：影片模型路線看起來更端到端，拆開之後，會不會顯得不夠新穎、繞開了更難的問題？ 最後，討論回到了目標：他們希望做的是一個有明確規則、能夠持續互動的世界。沿著這個目標，顯式狀態值得認真研究。 Project Eden釋出後，Code World Model、AgentGarten等工作也探索了由程式碼、引擎或智慧體維護狀態，再由影片模型生成畫面的分工；李飛飛團隊提出的“三層”世界模型架構、谷歌新發布的世界模型Genie 4，路線也與Project Eden形成了呼應。 △Genie 4將“程式碼和LLM負責邏輯結構化推理，生成模型負責渲染和表徵”的路線寫進未來規劃 分鐘級連續即時生成已經是一大突破，更長時間的一致性、更準確的控制，以及即時性與計算成本之間的取捨，是下一階段的課題。 讓年輕研究者定義問題，主導自己的代表作 這次V·STAR開放3D生成基礎模型、三維理解與智慧體、世界模型三個研究方向。 這些工作既需要不同背景的人交流，也需要研究者在尚無定論時作出判斷：現有路線的侷限在哪裡？什麼問題值得重新定義？是否應該嘗試一種不同的解法？對年輕人而言，關鍵不僅是能提出想法，還在於有沒有機會主導驗證。 Tripo P系列核心貢獻者Ronnie很早就來到VAST實習，畢業後正式加入。P系列的起點，正是他在實習期間提出的一次路線判斷。 當時，受大語言模型成功的影響，不少研究者嘗試用自迴歸方式生成原生網格，也已經做出了具有一定生產價值的結果。但Ronnie注意到，將三維網格強行轉化為序列，會損失資訊；隨著生成要求提高，這種表達方式的侷限可能進一步放大。 他因此提出：能不能換一條路，用擴散模型實現網格生成？ 彼時，行業中鮮有人探索這一方向，也沒有成熟路徑可循。但這個想法很快獲得了內部支援，Ronnie得以繼續推進實驗。 “我們有很多試錯和成長的機會，”他回憶，“可以自己做一些out of the box的探索。” 最初，他並沒有預設要做出一條旗艦產品線。但從識別現有方法的侷限，到提出替代路線，再到一步步驗證，研究探索最終發展成了Tripo P系列。 他獲得的不只是參與專案的機會，更是讓自己的技術判斷影響模型方向、將其做成代表作的空間。 他印象很深的一次反饋，發生在今年3月的舊金山遊戲開發者大會（GDC）。一位路過的遊戲開發者看完P1.0演示，驚訝於它展現的能力，表示此前沒有見過類似的東西。 △GDC上P1.0廣受歡迎 對研究者來說，這樣的反應很具體：自己在實驗裡反覆琢磨的東西，真的讓另一個人看到了新的創作可能。後來，開發者把模型接進不同Agent，做出團隊未曾設想過的作品，這份成就感又往前走了一步。 讓這樣的探索發生，除了給年輕人空間，還需要什麼支援？ EdenLive核心貢獻者之一Zion的經歷，提供了另一份回答。 他在VAST早期實習後，曾去大廠的大模型團隊實習半年，也拿到了大廠人才計劃的留用機會，最終卻在校招時回到VAST。 他沒有把這個選擇簡單歸納成“大廠和創業公司誰更好”。對他來說，重要的是能否探索自己關心的問題，以及探索所需的條件能否跟上。 回到VAST後，他得到充足的資料、基礎設施與算力支援，也逐漸明確了自己的研究目標：互動與模擬。 被問到再選一次是否還會來，他說：“我應該會比當時更加堅定。” 理由也很樸素：“當時期望的東西，在這不到一年裡確實都得到了回應。” 重要的判斷，不只發生在選擇路線時，也發生在實驗之後：哪些值得繼續，哪些需要調整，哪些應該暫時停下。 Zion曾嘗試讓LLM或VLM Agent結合3D生成搭建場景，但當時的基礎模型即便知道物體朝向不對，也難以穩定地將它轉正。驗證一段時間後，課題被暫時停下。 團隊先用有限資源檢驗關鍵假設，結果成立再繼續投入，不成立就重新討論。允許試錯，也包括允許研究者根據證據改變自己的判斷。 主導自己的研究，並不等於獨自解決所有問題。 VAST演算法團隊成員R期待的夥伴，是“high capability、low ego”：能力強，也願意把注意力放在共同解決問題上。仍在讀博的實習生Stewie，則已經參與核心模型從資料到訓練的完整流程。 在他的體驗裡，同伴願意分享理解、一起拆解難題，高人才密度帶來的也可以是支援。 這些經歷，對應著V·STAR希望提供的研究條件：入選者能夠從零推動專案，參與定義重點技術方向，獲得配套的資料、算力與協作支援。 待遇方面，薪酬突破傳統校招職級與薪資限制，特別優秀者上不封頂，並提供長期期權激勵。 在人才評價上，團隊更關注一項研究有沒有實質推進問題，研究者能否講清楚：為什麼值得做，為什麼選擇這條路線，實驗又怎樣改變了自己的判斷。 這也回應了開頭的難題：企業看重成果，人才計劃就不能只等待年輕人帶著代表作加入，還要提供讓代表作在這裡發生的條件——讓他們進入核心專案，作出重要判斷，並有資源和夥伴一起完成驗證。 從3D生成到世界模型，還有許多問題尚無定論。VAST希望新加入的年輕研究者，不只是參與尋找答案，也能一起決定，下一步該問什麼。 V·STAR校招面向2027屆本、碩、博畢業生，實習面向非應屆在校學生，不限年級。工作地點包括北京、杭州、上海、深圳及海外遠端。 官方通道： https:// tripo3d.com/vstar 投遞郵箱：vstar.talent@vastai3d.com title: Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.
abstract: Studio Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work. Back to Blog 7 min read Share this post Copy url to clipboard Copied Thinking Summary Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) enhances enterprise AI with advanced coding, cybersecurity, and document reasoning, while Mistral Studio provides a flexible platform for deploying agents, workflows, and apps across cloud, VPC, or on-premises environments. New features like managed agents, workflows, and enterprise context streamline business processes, enabling faster development and deployment of AI solutions. Customers like ABANCA and BNP Paribas already use Studio to automate tasks, improve efficiency, and maintain full control over their AI systems. Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) pushes the frontier of what enterprises can build with open models. It does great for coding , delivers advanced defensive cybersecurity capabilities , and brings powerful reasoning to complex documents and business tasks . Mistral Studio is our enterprise AI platform for putting that intelligence to work in your business. It lets your teams activate models quickly through agents, workflows and apps connected to your enterprise data and systems. Deploy them wherever you choose: in the cloud, in your own VPC, on-premises or across a combination of environments. And retain full control and understanding of the intelligence you create, from how your systems work to the knowledge they build. Today, we’re expanding Studio with managed agents and apps, alongside new capabilities for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability and evaluations. Customers and partners including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM and Tata Consultancy Services already use Studio in production. With this release, your developers can build and deploy new use cases faster, then reuse that work across more of the business. Mistral Studio is our platform for building enterprise AI applications. Running it in our own cloud environment, with inference provided by Mistral, allows us to bring AI into the business while retaining control over our infrastructure and how sensitive customer data is accessed and used. Jose Jorge Garcia Romaris, Head of Data Engineering & AI Our clients are looking beyond isolated AI use cases to reinvent how work gets done across the enterprise. Mistral Studio gives us the foundation to build, orchestrate and scale AI solutions tailored to their business needs, while securing control over their data and deployment. Combined with our industry expertise and delivery capabilities, it allows us to turn technology into real business impact at scale. Gregory Christophe, Accenture x Mistral Business Group Most industrial AI projects still stall at the pilot stage. We'll build agents and workflows for our clients' engineering and R&D teams on Mistral Studio to take their pilots into production. We're training our developers on the platform. Gualtiero Bazzana, ExCom Member and CAIO The AI systems we build run some of our most sensitive processes, so we run Mistral Studio on our own infrastructure and keep those systems under our control. Su YANG - Head of Artificial Intelligence & IT Innovation, BNP Paribas AI creates lasting value only when enterprises can trust it within their operations. Mistral Studio aims to let us decide exactly which systems the agents can access, and brings the observability and evaluation needed to turn a promising PoC into a system they can operate, measure, and rely on. That’s one of the gaps our clients are looking to close leveraging Mistral. Fernando Alvarez, Capgemini Group Chief Strategy & Development Officer, Group Executive Board Member We've built AI systems with Mistral's engineers for some of our most critical processes, from cargo release and customer assistance in shipping to transport orders in logistics. They run on Mistral Studio, where each new process we automate is production-ready in weeks rather than months. With the new version of Studio, our own teams and partners will do more of the building themselves, so we can take more of our processes to production and keep the know-how in-house. Julien Smadja, VP AI The future of enterprise AI will be defined by an ecosystem that balances innovation with trust, giving organizations the flexibility to adopt the right AI technologies while maintaining control. Through our partnership with Mistral, TCS is helping enterprises harness advanced AI capabilities while maintaining sovereignty, governance, security, and deployment flexibility. As one of the first global systems integrators investing in the Mistral ecosystem, we are enabling clients to build, deploy, govern, and scale AI with confidence. Together, we are accelerating the adoption of trusted AI and helping enterprises convert AI ambition into business outcomes. Amit Kapur, Chief AI & Services Transformation Officer Agents, workflows and apps for your business processes Agents, workflows and apps serve different parts of a business process. An agent investigates and acts, a workflow coordinates execution and approvals, and an app gives employees a way to use these systems. Studio brings all three together on shared infrastructure. You start with a model like Le Chonk and connect it to your enterprise data and systems through connectors and MCP servers. That foundation lets you easily build agents, workflows and apps with access to the context they need. Studio manages how they run and lets teams inspect what happened. Through the new Mistral MCP server, developers can build with Mistral Vibe or the coding agent they already use, test locally and deploy to their Studio environment with one command. Studio handles hosting and execution, so teams can build on that foundation to get each new use case into production faster. Build managed agents that investigate and act In Studio, developers can now build agents that carry out complex, multi-step tasks. Developers can equip them with skills that capture the team’s procedures, sandboxes where they can run code, and subagents to delegate parts of a task. Hooks let developers add custom logic at key points in execution, shaping how the agent works and integrates with existing systems. Studio manages the runtime behind all that work, using the proven infrastructure that supports millions of Mistral Vibe sessions each week. Developers can focus on the agent’s capabilities and behaviour, while setting boundaries on the tools, data and actions it can access. That means getting capable agents into production faster, with less infrastructure to build and more control over how your agents operate. Our engineering team built an agent in Studio to investigate production incidents. When an alert fires, engineers need to work out what happened, often under pressure to resolve the issue. The agent starts the investigation: it follows the team’s runbook, asks for approval before taking sensitive actions and posts its findings in Slack. Engineers pick up the investigation with useful context already gathered, saving the team hundreds of hours each month. Automate processes with workflows Workflows define how a process runs: which steps follow fixed rules, where an agent reasons and when a person decides. Interrupted runs can resume where they left off. Teams can describe a process in Mistral Vibe and use it to generate, test and deploy a workflow, with code they can inspect and edit. Today’s release also adds event triggers from enterprise systems and a visual graph that makes each workflow’s logic easier to inspect. Our product operations team built a workflow in Studio to sort ideas from internal teams and feedback from customers. Routing each submission to the right people is one of the team’s routine tasks, but one that takes time. A model identifies bugs and feature requests, then routing rules send them to the appropriate team. This saves the product operations team about 35 hours a week.

title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
abstract: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips Nov 05, 2026 | Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings 15-second clips, stronger consistency, and faster, more cost-effective generation. Anish Nangia Product Manager, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, which offers native 15-second video creation, improved reference adherence, and multi-turn conversational editing. This update lowers costs by 30% and provides better consistency for your professional projects. You can start using these capabilities today across the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business to produce high-quality video content at scale. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are launching Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with support for fifteen-second videos and improved reference adherence. You can now edit clips through multi-turn conversations, which allows for faster adjustments without starting over. We reduced the price by 30% to help you produce high-quality video content at a lower cost. This model is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud for your production needs. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business . Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video. Here’s an overview of what’s new: Fast and cost-effective at scale Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K. Longer clips up to 15 seconds You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation. Better reference adherence You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads. Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent. More consistent results You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot. Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame. Easier editing in conversation You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating. Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact. More natural speech You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow , creating video explainers in Gemini for business , or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids . Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene. More controllable, cinematic look You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look. Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts. Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts. 15 second long clips: Turns one style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer with accurately spelled, motion-tracked callouts. Multi-turn motion transfer: Generates a rippling octopus in Turn 1, then replaces it in Turn 2 with a dancer whose gown mirrors the exact fluid motion. First-to-last frame consistency (1.1 vs. 1.2): Connects an exterior start frame and interior end frame in one continuous camera push in 1.2 Flash. You can see subtle differences like the cats on the roof, the soup ladle turning into chopsticks, and some other minor changes. Unbroken crash zoom-out: Pulls continuously from a tight shoreline close-up to an aerial island vista in one 10-second shot with natural scale and zero cuts. Real-world results, from creatives to global brands Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark. Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms: For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio , explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing . For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console , and build enterprise solutions with the API .

title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
abstract: Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan.

title: Hamed Karimi wins ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award
abstract: In Naples last month, at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD), Amazon senior applied scientist Hamed Karimi and colleagues won the 2026 ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award for their 2016 paper “Linear convergence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition”. The award recognizes research published a decade earlier that has had a lasting impact. The paper, written with Julie Nutini and Mark Schmidt while Karimi was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia, has helped to organize a previously scattered field of machine learning optimization and offers useful approaches to analyzing new training methods. “When we wrote the paper in 2016, we genuinely didn’t expect it to make a splash,” Karimi says. “We did not know that the result would become part of the way researchers analyze optimization in machine learning.” Karimi and his coauthors showed that the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, a 1963 mathematical inequality that had been largely overlooked in machine learning, can prove that the standard method for training machine learning models closes in on the best solutions quickly, even when many different solutions could work equally well. Because modern machine learning models rarely have a single best solution, the result helped close a long-standing gap between what training methods do in practice and what theory could guarantee. Optimization landscape In the classic supervised-machine-learning setting, a model’s billions of settings, or parameters, are adjusted so that the model’s outputs match labeled training data as closely as possible. The distance between the model’s output and the labeled data is measured with a loss function; the goal is to tune the parameters to minimize the loss. This tuning is done through optimization processes, the most common approach being gradient descent or one of its variants. One way to understand gradient descent is to visualize a topographic map with peaks, valleys, cliffs, and plateaus. The lowest points on the map represent minimal loss, with each step downhill toward these minima representing parameter adjustments that optimize toward fewer errors. Ideally, researchers would like to know the quickest path to the bottom. Theory suggests that the fastest path shrinks the error by a constant fraction each step, a property known as linear convergence. The problem is that linear convergence is mathematically guaranteed only for a particular topographic shape: a steep bowl that uniformly curves upward, one that is strongly convex. A bowl like this has exactly one lowest point, so from any location, there is a single best move toward optimization. But many real problems don't work that way. When training data are redundant, as is the case with modern large language models, where the parameter count is disproportionately large compared to the amount of training data, the bottom of the landscape becomes a flat valley floor instead of a single point at the bottom of a bowl. These models — which exhibit weaker conditions than convexity — can be successfully trained with gradient descent, but the theory could neither explain why nor say how quickly, leaving a gap between what works in practice and what can be proven. By 2016, some 25 years’ worth of solutions to optimization problems with weaker conditions were in circulation, each with its own name, notation, and paper, but nobody had established how they related. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper settled those relationships. Researchers have since used variations of the paper’s method to rederive guarantees for essentially every standard optimization algorithm in machine learning. The paper has been cited over 2,000 times and has found a place in graduate textbooks. Tying it together At the center of the paper is the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, an inequality published in 1963 by Boris Polyak in a Russian-language paper on gradient methods and by Stanisław Łojasiewicz in French that same year, independently and for unrelated reasons; Polyak was studying optimization, Łojasiewicz real analytic geometry. In the paper, Karimi and coauthors named the condition after both. If the condition holds, then even though the problem doesn’t exhibit a strongly convex geometry, the optimization is still guaranteed to converge at a linear rate. The proof of this is only three lines long. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper made three contributions. The first was a map of existing solutions for problems with weaker conditions, all of which make different assumptions about problem topology. For smooth functions that need not be convex, the researchers worked out every implication of competing assumptions, from strongest to weakest. For most of these functions, linear convergence had been proved before, but only in the convex case. Before Karimi and his colleagues’ work, little was understood about how these competing approaches related to one another. The map gave researchers a clear picture of the existing methods, showing which assumptions imply which, and identified the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition as the weakest of the known conditions that still guarantees a linear rate. The second contribution extended the results to landscapes that combine a smooth function — one that slopes gradually and predictably at all points — with nonsmooth ones — those with corners, kinks, or edges, points where the slope is undefined. The paper introduced a variant of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition that guarantees the same linear rate, bringing many widely used models under the same short analysis. The third contribution was a reanalysis of the standard optimization algorithms, variants of gradient descent that include coordinate descent, sign gradient descent, and stochastic gradient descent. In each case, the analysis recovered the rate of convergence previously known only for strongly convex functions. In other words, the same short argument gives researchers a ready-made template for analyzing new training methods as they appear. Rate of influence Two weeks after the preprint was posted, Polyak wrote the authors. “Actually, it was a surprise for me why the simple condition from my old publication attracted so little attention,” he said, “and now your work exhibits its importance.” He attached an English translation of his 1963 paper, largely unused in the five decades since. Karimi sees two reasons the condition has spread so far over the past decade. First, adopting it took almost no work. Many existing proofs that assumed the idealized bowl shape relied on just one consequence of it: loss, wherever it was measured in the landscape, would still be well above its minimum value. In other words, the ground slopes steeply enough to make real progress downhill. The Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition guarantees exactly that property, so those proofs still hold when the condition is swapped in. Second, and most consequentially, it made fast convergence on a nonconvex problem a provable statement, which is now part of how the field explains why the algorithms researchers run in practice work so well. The condition has also traveled well beyond the setting that Karimi and his colleagues studied. Variants now support convergence results in reinforcement learning, optimization over curved parameter spaces, and the sampling methods behind diffusion models. Ten years on, an inequality that sat unused for five decades has become one of the standard assumptions in the analysis of optimization methods for machine learning.

title: A builder’s guide to scaling Databricks Apps
abstract: Congratulations, you've built an app on Databricks Apps, and it's gone from a couple of users to hundreds or thousands across your organization. Your users want it to respond fast and stay up. And your boss may not love having to pay for XLarge compute across a stack of instances. How do you make an app that runs fast, stays up and handles growing demand? The intuitive answer is more compute, but that only helps once you know where requests spend their time and whether the app is built to scale: its framework, async code and ability to run on several instances, so the platform can easily scale it up or out. In this guide, we walk through how to scale Databricks Apps across four stages: design; build; test and deploy; and operate (Figure 1). The focus of this guide is primarily application performance and resiliency at scale; it does not cover deployment automation or performance optimization and scaling of other Databricks services that may interact with the app. Figure 1: Four stages of scaling a Databricks App. Good scaling decisions start before any code is written: agree what users need from the app, then decide where the work will run and where the data will live. Before choosing an architecture, it helps to pin down how much load the app has to handle and what a good experience looks like. We suggest agreeing two main targets: Alongside these, decide which work must survive a restart and check that critical dependencies can support that. This shapes how you split state and how many instances you run. Next, sketch a few user journeys, such as opening a dashboard or submitting a question. For each action, note the services it calls, roughly how many calls it makes and which depend on each other, how fast it should finish and how stale cached data can be. These assumptions shape the architecture and the first test targets. Once a prototype runs, you can measure the real calls and revise them. Suppose a retailer gives its 2,000 store managers an app to check stock, backed by Lakebase. During the busiest hour of Black Friday, 200 of them are using it at once. If each makes two stock checks per minute on average, that is 400 checks per minute. If each check executes three SQL statements against Lakebase, expect 1,200 statements per minute, or 20 per second on average during that hour. This estimates query rate, not concurrency. Test bursts and growth, validate against live usage, and budget connections separately (see "Budget the connections to Lakebase"). App compute is there to serve the UI and coordinate calls, not to do the heavy lifting. We recommend sending each kind of work to the service built for it (Figure 2). For long-running calls, run the work in the background, for example as a job, and let the UI poll for status or receive streamed updates, rather than holding one request open until it finishes. If the app needs to run code it doesn't control, such as code written by users or generated by an agent, don't run it in the app. Run it in Databricks Sandbox , an isolated environment that can start from a custom image, so its CPU and memory use stays off the instances serving users. Figure 2: Where each kind of work runs and where the state lives. When more people use your app, you can add capacity in two ways: scale up (vertical scaling) by moving to a larger compute size, which gives each instance more CPU and memory, or scale out (horizontal scaling) by adding instances to share the request load. With heavy work running outside the app, what usually limits it is how many requests it can handle at once. For example, in the Black Friday case, each stock check is light, but checks from 200 store managers can arrive together in bursts. More instances spread those requests, and a larger instance helps if the app can use the extra cores, typically by running more workers. An app that keeps a large reference dataset or model in memory hits a different limit. A larger instance gives it the memory it needs; adding instances doesn't help, because each instance loads its own copy. You can start on Medium and let the load test later in this guide show which you need. The framework is harder to change later, so it's worth choosing now. Databricks Apps runs apps built on Python or Node.js and you aren't limited to the frameworks below. For most new apps, we recommend AppKit , the TypeScript SDK that databricks apps init and the Databricks agent skills use by default. Caching, telemetry, retry logic and error handling come built in, giving you a starting point for several practices in this guide. AppKit runs one Node.js process per instance by default, so the simplest way to scale is by adding instances. If you already have an app, or your back end needs Python: Whichever you choose, if it keeps session state in server memory, it's worth testing what happens when a session moves to another instance before you scale out. Most Databricks Apps keep some state in memory, and that's fine as long as you know which parts you can afford to lose. A useful first step is to list what each session holds and what must survive a restart, then split it into soft and hard state: How that split works depends on the kind of app: Figure 3: When a session moves, another instance can rebuild it from hard state. Databricks Apps keeps each user on the same instance on a best-effort basis (session affinity) and rebalances sessions when needed, so any per-user cache your app keeps locally usually stays available. Restarts, failures and scaling changes can still move a session, so another instance must be able to rebuild it from hard state (Figure 3). With targets and an architecture in place, the next step is code that holds up under load, including when a session moves or an instance stops. We recommend turning on telemetry from the start, so the data is there before you need it. App telemetry writes logs, traces and metrics to Unity Catalog tables through OpenTelemetry. Once it's enabled for an app, logs arrive automatically, but traces and metrics need instrumentation. You should create custom spans around SQL, database, model and API calls to show where the time goes. Record caught exceptions on the span as well, so they show up in your traces. Trace and request IDs then let you follow one user's requests across instances. For example, a span around a SQL call: Most apps spend their time waiting on another service: a SQL query, a model call, an external API. With blocking calls, each wait holds an execution slot for the whole call. A handful of slow calls can exhaust that capacity. That's why async handlers matter for I/O-heavy work. When handlers await model and database calls, one worker can keep serving other requests while it waits, as long as those calls are non-blocking. Your traces and system metrics will show when this applies: if most of a request's time is spent in SQL, model or API spans, and latency rises with concurrent users while CPU stays low, requests are likely queuing behind blocking calls. Even with async, one request can still be slow if it runs its queries one after another. Start independent queries together (for example, with asyncio.gather or Promise.all ), so the request takes close to as long as its slowest query. It's also worth capping how many run in parallel, so one request can't flood the warehouse or database. Often it is better to combine queries than to run N+1 queries, where the app fetches a list and then runs one more query per item: a join or an IN clause does the same work in one or two. A cache speeds up an app, but it can also leak data: an app-level cache doesn't enforce Unity Catalog permissions, so a shared cache can show one user another user's data. Scope cache keys by the user's verified identity and the query parameters, and by session where needed; never key on an identity the client sends without verifying it. Share cached data only when it's identical for everyone.

title: Which Data Collaboration Tool: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms, Marketplace
abstract: The world of sharing has extended far past tables. We can now securely share all kinds of data and AI assets, from models to notebooks to AI agents, and the appetite to do so only keeps growing. While in the past, it may have been difficult to get just a table to or from a partnering business, these days it's easier than ever to provide access. With this growing demand, we have seen three methods of sharing pop up in Databricks: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms, and Marketplace. With the emergence of these three, the question arises: “When do I use one over the other?” Picking the wrong one can cost you a wasted engineering sprint, or worse, expose data you meant to keep protected. In this blog, we'll dive into the three different sharing options and how they can apply to your business and your partnerships. As we'll see, the right choice usually comes down to one thing: the relationship you have with whoever is on the other side of the data. First, we have OpenSharing, the simplest way to share data assets. Essentially, you create a share, associate assets with it, and provide access to that share to recipients. OpenSharing will handle the access, even if that recipient isn't on Databricks. This changes the paradigm as you no longer need to stand up pipelines to ship data to each consumer. Instead, consumers get direct read-only access to the original live asset once you've granted it, so what they see is always up to date. Even popular BI tools like Power BI and Tableau can read directly from OpenShared tables. So a partner can directly connect their BI to the data you share with them. You may have noticed I used the word “data assets." That is because you can share more than just tables with businesses outside your organization, including tables (Delta or Iceberg), Views, Volumes, Notebooks, UDFs, and even AI Models. This is also not limited to outside organizations; several businesses use OpenSharing to share data with different business units. Across industries, we have seen businesses utilize or ingest data from partnered businesses via OpenSharing: You might be thinking you could do this yourself by standing up a pipeline to share data out and managing credentials. And you would be correct, but the point of OpenSharing is to remove that overhead. You do not need to make copies of your data and spend unnecessary money. You share in minutes, and revoke just as fast. Next, we have the Databricks Clean Rooms, which is much like it sounds: a sealed, neutral space where two or more businesses (up to ten) can bring their data together and run only the code every party has approved. Everyone benefits from the results, but no one ever sees another party's full underlying data. Let's say my company has proprietary data, and a business we partner with frequently has data they want to marry with ours to maximize value. Neither of us wants to share a full dataset, but we believe there is value in sharing snippets of data or joining our data on select fields. Instead of sending the full dataset over, we both share our table’s names and columns with each other and collaborate on authoring a notebook. For anything to run, we both have to give a thumbs-up of approval. That, in essence, is how Clean Rooms operate. They let us collaborate with another business and intermingle data that is proprietary to each of us, while limiting what we share to only what we agreed to in that handshake. This is extremely common across a few industries: Reach for a clean room when combining data is valuable, but neither side wants to expose its full underlying data. The key difference is that, rather than giving the recipient direct access to the object itself, you only see the results of code that both sides have approved. Last, we have the Databricks Marketplace. Think of it as a public storefront where you can share Files, Tables, Models, MCP (Model Context Protocol) Servers, Notebooks, Apps, and SaaS software. OpenSharing and Clean Rooms are options when you have an existing relationship with your customer. The Databricks Marketplace is about the ones you do not. It is an open exchange where data providers, software vendors, and technology partners publish offerings that any Databricks customer can discover, evaluate, and connect to directly from their workspace. If you are a provider, it is a storefront that puts your assets in front of a broad audience. On the other side, if you are a consumer, you can find data and AI products to plug into your own work. Either way, what sets Marketplace apart is that it is public and discoverable: with OpenSharing and Clean Rooms, you already know who is on the other side, but on Marketplace, anyone can find your listing without you ever having met them. Common examples of Marketplace: Reach for Marketplace when you do not have a specific recipient in mind: you either want to be found, or you want to go find data and AI products yourself. If you are still on the fence about which approach to use, let the relationship decide. If you already know exactly who should receive the data and you're comfortable sharing a read-only version, reach for OpenSharing. If you have a specific partner but neither side wants to expose its full underlying data, use a Clean Room. And if you don't have a specific recipient yet but want to be discovered, or you want to discover data and AI products yourself, that's Marketplace. Lastly, these are not mutually exclusive; the same business can use different tools for different relationships. At the end of the day, these are all tools meant to enable your business and prevent slowdown from the traditional burdens of data sharing. So if you ever have customers asking for data, think about the relationship and match it to the right tool! Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: From Delta Sharing to OpenSharing: what changed, what's next
abstract: Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across clouds and platforms without copying it. In June 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced that Delta Sharing has evolved into OpenSharing , an open, vendor-neutral protocol for sharing not just tables, but the broader set of assets that AI teams now depend on: agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data. If you already share data with Delta Sharing, or you're evaluating how to collaborate with partners on both data and AI assets, this post walks through what OpenSharing actually is, what's changed under the hood, and where the project is headed. When Databricks introduced Delta Sharing at Data + AI Summit 2021, the core problem it addressed was simple to state and hard to solve well: organizations wanted to share live data with partners, customers, and other teams, without exporting files, standing up brittle ETL jobs, or forcing every recipient onto the same platform. Delta Sharing was contributed to the Linux Foundation as an open protocol, built on Delta Lake and Parquet, so a provider could grant access to a table and a recipient could query it directly, in real time, from tools like Apache Spark, Power BI, Tableau, pandas, and many others. That open, zero-copy model resonated. Delta Sharing grew into the most widely adopted open protocol for secure data sharing, used by organizations including Amadeus, Atlassian, LSEG, SAP, Stripe, and The Trade Desk for cross-cloud and cross-platform collaboration, according to Databricks ( Databricks press release ). By the time Databricks announced OpenSharing in June 2026, Delta Sharing had reached more than 28,000 data recipients, with roughly a third of shares flowing across platforms through open connectors rather than staying inside Databricks-to-Databricks sharing ( Databricks blog ). Sharing had already grown well beyond tables. Through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, teams were exchanging views, volumes of unstructured files, notebooks, and registered ML models years before agents entered the picture, so structured data was never the whole story. What agents changed was the kind of asset that needed to move, and how far it needed to travel. Agent skills, the agents themselves, and the semantic context they run on all called for the same governed, zero-copy access that sharing had already proven out. Enterprises also wanted that access to reach across platforms and beyond Databricks-to-Databricks connections, and the open protocol still centered on tables, so these newer assets sat outside what open, cross-platform sharing could actually deliver. At the same time, enterprises kept asking for two related things: broader interoperability with formats like Apache Iceberg, and a way to bring data that lives on premises or in private clouds into the same governed sharing model, without migrating it first. Addressing both of these gaps meant rethinking Delta Sharing's scope, not just adding features to it. On June 10, 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation jointly announced OpenSharing as the next evolution of Delta Sharing ( Databricks press release , Linux Foundation press release ). Precision matters here, because OpenSharing operates at two distinct layers: The open ecosystem reaches beyond the protocol itself. Open source Unity Catalog, an Apache 2.0 project also governed under the Linux Foundation, provides a vendor-neutral catalog and governance layer for these assets, so a team can pair it with an open sharing server and run governed sharing entirely outside Databricks ( GitHub, Unity Catalog ). Databricks Co-founder and CTO Matei Zaharia framed the move this way: "Delta Sharing proved the industry would choose open over locked-in. OpenSharing extends that principle to the full AI stack, while expanding the cross-platform ecosystem to Iceberg recipients and on-premises providers" ( Databricks press release ). Linux Foundation CEO Jim Zemlin added that the goal is "a common, vendor-neutral framework that enables organizations to exchange AI assets securely and interoperably across platforms and ecosystems" ( Linux Foundation press release ). One clarification worth making up front: existing Delta Sharing clients and integrations remain compatible with OpenSharing. This is an evolution of the protocol, not a break from it, and the delta-io/delta-sharing repository continues to exist alongside the new OpenSharing-IO/OpenSharing GitHub organization. Diagram: Delta Sharing evolves into OpenSharing, which operates as an open protocol layer on GitHub plus a Databricks enterprise implementation layer, with new reach into Iceberg REST Catalog clients and on-premises or private cloud storage. A broader asset model. The original open Delta Sharing protocol centered on tables, even as Databricks-to-Databricks sharing had grown to cover more asset types. OpenSharing brings that broader model into the open specification itself and introduces a Share → Schema → Asset hierarchy that extends sharing beyond Tables to new asset types, including Volumes (directories of files in any format), Agent Skills, and AI models ( GitHub, OpenSharing ). This means a provider can package a data product that includes both the underlying tables and the AI assets built on top of them, and share the whole thing through one protocol. Diagram: OpenSharing's asset hierarchy. Table, Volume, Agent Skill, and Model are specified asset types today. Agent and Page or Glossary types are listed as community proposals still under discussion. Iceberg REST Catalog support. OpenSharing adds support for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) compatible clients, so providers can share data to any Iceberg-compatible engine, not only Delta Sharing native clients. Databricks describes this as extending the reach of open sharing to organizations standardized on Iceberg tooling ( Databricks product page ). On-premises and private cloud reach.
